label: prop:support-separation
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:support-separation}
  Let $k\ge6$ be an integer and $x=\beta_k$.
  Suppose that $\mathsf P$ maximizes $F_k$ among nonnegative Borel probability laws of mean at most $x$.
  Write $\mathsf P=(1-kx)\delta_0+kx\mathsf Q$, where $\mathsf Q\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])$ has mean $1/k$.
    For independent $Y_1,\ldots,Y_k$ with law $\mathsf Q$, set $w=k\mathbb{E}(Y_1+\cdots+Y_k-1)_+$ and assume $0<w<W_k$.
  Then $\mathsf P([x+D/16,x+17D/20])=0$ and $\mathsf P((x+17D/20,M])>0$.
head: environment

label: lem:normal-comparison
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:normal-comparison}
  Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, and let $\widetilde Z_1,\ldots,\widetilde Z_n$ be independent and identically distributed random variables with mean zero, positive variance, and finite third absolute moment.
  Write $U=\sum_{i=1}^n\widetilde Z_i$, $s^2=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb{E}\widetilde Z_i^2$, and $B_3=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb{E}|\widetilde Z_i|^3$.
  For every $t\in\mathbb R$, we have
  \[
    \left|\mathbb{P}(U<t)-\Phi(t/s)\right|
    \le
    0.3328\left(
    \frac{B_3}{s^3}+\frac{0.429}{\sqrt n}
    \right)
    \le\frac{B_3}{3s^3}+\frac1{7\sqrt n}.
  \]
head: environment
name: Shevtsova

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $d=D/x$, $\mu=(M-r)/D$, and $v=\operatorname{Var}(S_k\mid S_k<1)$.
  By {\cref{prop:finite-shortfall-margin}\textup{\ref{item:shortfall-margin}}},
  \[
    0\le M-r<\frac{D-3x}{20}.
  \]
  Consequently, $d>3$ and
  \[
    0\le\mu<\mu_0:=\frac{d-3}{20d}<\frac1{20}.
  \]

  We first prove that $\mathsf P([x+D/16,x+17D/20])=0$.
  By {\cref{lem:contact-moment}\textup{\ref{item:contact-moment-bounds}}}, we have $v\le(r-\delta)(M-r)$.
  Since $M-r=\mu D$, $M=x+D$, $\delta=cx$, and $d=D/x$, we have $(r-\delta)/D=1-\mu+(1-c)/d$.
  Hence, using $c\ge11/24$,
  \[
    \frac v{D^2}
    \le\mu\left(1-\mu+\frac{1-c}{d}\right)
    \le\mu\left(1-\mu+\frac{13}{24d}\right).
  \]
  For fixed $d>3$, the function $u\mapsto u(1-u+13/(24d))$ is strictly increasing on $[0,1/20]$.
  Since $\mu<\mu_0$, we obtain
  \[
    \frac v{D^2}
    <\mu_0\left(1-\mu_0+\frac{13}{24d}\right)
    <\frac{19}{400}.
  \]

  Let $W$ have the distribution of $1-S_k$ conditional on $S_k<1$.
  Then $\mathbb{E} W=r$ and $\operatorname{Var}(W)=v$.
  Suppose, for a contradiction, that there exists $y\in[x+D/16,x+17D/20]$ such that
  \[
    \mathbb{P}(S_{k-1}<1-y)=p\frac{M-y}{D}.
  \]
  Write $y=x+\theta D$, where $1/16\le\theta\le17/20$.
  Since $\mu<1/20$, we have $r-y=(1-\mu-\theta)D>0$.
  Since $y>0$ and $S_{k-1}\le S_k$, it follows that
  \[
    \mathbb{P}(W>y)
    =\frac{\mathbb{P}(S_k<1-y)}p
    \le\frac{\mathbb{P}(S_{k-1}<1-y)}p
    =\frac{M-y}{D}
    =1-\theta.
  \]
  Since $r-y>0$, Cantelli's inequality gives
  \[
    \theta\le\mathbb{P}(W\le y)
    =\mathbb{P}(W-r\le-(r-y))
    \le\frac{v}{v+(r-y)^2}.
  \]
  Since $0<\theta<1$,
  \[
    \frac v{D^2}
    \ge
    \frac{\theta(1-\mu-\theta)^2}{1-\theta}
    \ge
    \frac{\theta(19/20-\theta)^2}{1-\theta}.
  \]
  The second inequality uses $\mu<1/20$ and $19/20-\theta>0$.

  Let $f(\theta)=\theta(19/20-\theta)^2/(1-\theta)$ for $1/16\le\theta\le17/20$.
  Then
  \[
    f'(\theta)
    =\frac{(19/20-\theta)(2\theta^2-3\theta+19/20)}
    {(1-\theta)^2}.
  \]
  Set $\theta_*=(15-\sqrt{35})/20$.
  We have $f'(\theta)>0$ for $1/16\le\theta<\theta_*$ and $f'(\theta)<0$ for $\theta_*<\theta\le17/20$.
  Since $f(1/16)=5041/96000$ and $f(17/20)=17/300$, we obtain
  \[
    \frac v{D^2}\ge f(\theta)
    \ge\min\{f(1/16),f(17/20)\}
    =\frac{5041}{96000}>\frac{19}{400},
  \]
  contrary to $v/D^2<19/400$.
  Thus, no $y\in[x+D/16,x+17D/20]$ satisfies $\mathbb{P}(S_{k-1}<1-y)=p(M-y)/D$.
  By {\cref{obs:contact-identities}\textup{\ref{item:contact-failure}}}, $\mathbb{P}(S_{k-1}<1-y)=p(M-y)/D$ holds for $\mathsf P$-almost every $y$, so $\mathsf P([x+D/16,x+17D/20])=0$.

  Suppose that $\mathsf P((x+17D/20,M])=0$.
  Then $\mathsf P([0,x+D/16))=1$.
  For $X\sim\mathsf P$, set $H=(X-x)/x$ and write $s^2=k\mathbb{E} H^2$ and $B_3=k\mathbb{E}|H|^3$.
  Then $\mathbb{E} H=0$ and $-1\le H\le d/16$ almost surely.
  By {\cref{cor:contact-moments}\textup{\ref{item:contact-moment-identity}}}, $c<1/2$, and $d\mu<(d-3)/20$,
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:variance-floor}
    s^2=d(d+1-c-d\mu)
    >d\left(\frac{19d}{20}+\frac{13}{20}\right).
  \end{equation}
  Since $d>3$, \eqref{eq:variance-floor} gives $s>3$ and $s>19d/20$.
  Thus, $0<c/s<1/6$ and $B_3/s^3\le\max\{1,d/16\}/s$.
  The standard normal density exceeds $1/3$ on $[0,1/6]$, so $\Phi(-t)\le1/2-t/3$ for $0\le t\le1/6$.

  For $1\le i\le k$, set $H_i=(X_i-x)/x$.
  Then $S_k\ge1$ if and only if $\sum_{i=1}^kH_i\ge c$.
  Lyapunov's inequality gives $B_3/s^3\ge1/\sqrt{k}$.
  Hence, $B_3/(3s^3)+1/(7\sqrt{k})\le10B_3/(21s^3)<B_3/(2s^3)$.
    By \cref{lem:normal-comparison} and a straightforward calculation using $c>11/24$, $s>3$, and $s>19d/20$, we obtain
    \[
      \begin{aligned}
        F_k(\mathsf P)
         & =\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^kH_i\ge c\right) \\
         & \le\Phi(-c/s)+\frac{B_3}{2s^3}<\frac58.
      \end{aligned}
    \]
  But maximality and {\cref{lem:sec4-parameter-bounds}} give $F_k(\mathsf P)\ge a^k=1-p_0>5/8$, a contradiction.

label: lem:upper-intensity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:upper-intensity}
  Let $k\ge6$ be an integer, $11/24\le c\le1/2$, $x=(k+c)^{-1}$, and $x<M\le1$.
  Suppose that $0\le\varepsilon\le1/10$ and $\zeta=17/20$.
  Let $\mathsf P$ be a probability distribution of mean $x$, supported on $[0,x+\varepsilon D]\cup(x+\zeta D,M]$, with $\mathsf P((x+\zeta D,M])>0$.
  Assume that $p\le p_0$, $D>3x$, and $r\le M$.
  Suppose also that $\operatorname{Var}(S_k)=D(r-\delta)$ and $\mathbb{P}(S_{k-1}<1-y)=p(M-y)/D$ for $\mathsf P$-almost every $y$.
  Then the following statements hold.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item\label{item:upper-intensity-zero} If $x_0=0$, then $M=1$ and $\mathsf P=(1-x)\delta_0+x\delta_1=\mathsf B_x$.
    \item\label{item:upper-intensity-parameters} If $x_0>0$, then $J>m+\delta-x_0/5$ almost surely and
    \[
      0<a-\lambda\le\eta<a,\text{ }
      q\le\frac DA\text{ and }
      0\le\frac{\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}{A}<\frac{3D}{20A}.
    \]
    \item\label{item:upper-intensity-ratio} If $x_0>0$, then
    \[
      \frac{p_0A}{Dq^{k-1}}\le\mathrm{e}^{-(a-\lambda)}\le1.
    \]
  \end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: lem:positive-deficit-tail
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:positive-deficit-tail}
  Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent nonnegative random variables with $\mathbb{E} X_i\le1$ for every $i$.
  Write $S=X_1+\cdots+X_n$.
  Then $\mathbb{P}(S<\mathbb{E} S+v)>g(v)$ for every $v>0$.
head: environment
name: Fu, Han, Wang, Yan, Zhang and Zhou

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\operatorname{Var}(S_k)=D(r-\delta)$, $r\le M$, $d>3$, and $c\ge11/24$,
  \[
    \frac{\operatorname{Var}(S_k)}{D^2}
    \le1+\frac{1-c}{d}<\frac{85}{72}.
  \]
  By independence and $\mathsf P=q\mathsf{L}(X^{\operatorname{L}})+(1-q)\mathsf{L}(X^{\operatorname{U}})$,
  \[
    \operatorname{Var}(S_k)\ge k(1-q)q(\mathbb{E} X^{\operatorname{U}}-x_0)^2
    =\frac{\lambda}{q}(\mathbb{E} X^{\operatorname{U}}-x)^2.
  \]
  Here $\mathbb{E} X^{\operatorname{U}}-x=q(\mathbb{E} X^{\operatorname{U}}-x_0)>17D/20$.
  Hence, $\lambda/q<(85/72)(20/17)^2=250/153$.

  Since $\log q>-(1-q)/q$ and $\log p_0\le k\log((k-1/2)/(k+1/2))<-1$, we obtain
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:prelude-count-ratio}
    \frac{q^{k-1}}{p_0}
    >\exp\left(1-\frac{k-1}{k}\frac{\lambda}{q}\right)
    >\mathrm{e}^{1-250/153}.
  \end{equation}
  We will use
  \[
    \mathrm{e}^{1-250/153}g(11/24)
    >\frac{11}{24}\mathrm{e}^{-11/10}
    >\frac{11}{24}\cdot\frac4{11}\cdot\frac9{10}
    =\frac3{20},
  \]
  where the inequalities follow from $250/153+11/24<21/10$, $\mathrm{e}^{-1}>4/11$, and $\mathrm{e}^{-1/10}>9/10$.
  Since $g(11/24)<1$, we also have $\mathrm{e}^{1-250/153}>3/20$.

  For every $y\in\mathbb R$, in the representation $X_i=(1-I_i)X_i^{\operatorname{L}}+I_iX_i^{\operatorname{U}}$, the probability that all $k-1$ samples lie in $[0,x+\varepsilon D]$ and have sum less than $1-y$ is $q^{k-1}\mathbb{P}(X_1^{\operatorname{L}}+\cdots+X_{k-1}^{\operatorname{L}}<1-y)$.
  Thus, $q^{k-1}\mathbb{P}(X_1^{\operatorname{L}}+\cdots+X_{k-1}^{\operatorname{L}}<1-y)\le\mathbb{P}(S_{k-1}<1-y)$.
  Using $\mathbb{P}(S_{k-1}<1-y)=p(M-y)/D$ for $\mathsf P$-almost every $y$, we obtain, for $\mathsf{L}(X^{\operatorname{U}})$-almost every $y$,
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:prelude-contact}
    p\frac{M-y}{D}
    \ge q^{k-1}\mathbb{P}(B_{k-1}<1-y-(k-1)x_0).
  \end{equation}
  Since $x+17D/20<X^{\operatorname{U}}\le M$ almost surely and $D<A$,
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:prelude-raw-cap}
    \frac{M-X^{\operatorname{U}}}{D}<\frac3{20}
    \text{ and }
    \frac JA=1-\frac{M-X^{\operatorname{U}}}A>\frac{17}{20}
    \quad\text{almost surely.}
  \end{equation}

  First suppose that $x_0=0$.
  Then $X^{\operatorname{L}}=0$ and $B_{k-1}=0$ almost surely, so $\mathbb{P}(B_{k-1}<1-y)=1$ for every $y<1$.
  If $\mathbb{P}(X^{\operatorname{U}}<1)>0$, then \eqref{eq:prelude-contact}, \eqref{eq:prelude-count-ratio}, and $p\le p_0$ give
  \[
    \frac{M-y}D\ge\frac{q^{k-1}}p
    >\mathrm{e}^{1-250/153}>\frac3{20}
  \]
  for $\mathsf{L}(X^{\operatorname{U}})$-almost every $y<1$.
  After substituting $y=X^{\operatorname{U}}$, the preceding inequality holds almost surely on $\{X^{\operatorname{U}}<1\}$, contrary to \eqref{eq:prelude-raw-cap}.
  Hence, $\mathbb{P}(X^{\operatorname{U}}<1)=0$.
  Since $X^{\operatorname{U}}\le M\le1$, we have $X^{\operatorname{U}}=1$ almost surely and $M=1$.
  Taking means then gives $1-q=x$, so $\mathsf P=(1-x)\delta_0+x\delta_1$.

  Henceforth assume $x_0>0$.
  For every $y\in\mathbb R$, write $\vartheta_y=(1-y-(k-1)x_0)/x_0$.
  For every fixed $y$ with $\vartheta_y>0$, apply \cref{lem:positive-deficit-tail} to $X_1^{\operatorname{L}}/x_0,\ldots,X_{k-1}^{\operatorname{L}}/x_0$, which are independent, nonnegative, and have mean one.
  Since $(1-y)/x_0=(k-1)+\vartheta_y$, we obtain $\mathbb{P}(B_{k-1}<1-y-(k-1)x_0)>g(\vartheta_y)$.
  Combining $\mathbb{P}(B_{k-1}<1-y-(k-1)x_0)>g(\vartheta_y)$ with \eqref{eq:prelude-contact} and $p\le p_0$ gives, for $\mathsf{L}(X^{\operatorname{U}})$-almost every $y$ with $\vartheta_y>0$,
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:prelude-tail-comparison}
    \frac{M-y}{D}
    >\frac{q^{k-1}}{p_0}g(\vartheta_y).
  \end{equation}
  Since $X^{\operatorname{U}}=x_0+J$ and $1-kx_0=\delta+m$, we have $\vartheta_{X^{\operatorname{U}}}=(\delta+m-J)/x_0$.

  We claim that $J>m/a$ almost surely.
  If $\mathbb{P}(J\le m/a)>0$, then, since $\delta=cx_0+cm/k$ and $a^{-1}=1+c/k$,
  \[
    \vartheta_{X^{\operatorname{U}}}\ge\frac{\delta+m-m/a}{x_0}=c
  \]
  on $\{J\le m/a\}$.
  Since $g$ is nondecreasing, substituting $y=X^{\operatorname{U}}$ in \eqref{eq:prelude-tail-comparison} and using \eqref{eq:prelude-count-ratio} gives
  \[
    \frac{M-X^{\operatorname{U}}}D
    >\mathrm{e}^{1-250/153}g(c)
    \ge\mathrm{e}^{1-250/153}g(11/24)
    >\frac3{20}
  \]
  almost surely on $\{J\le m/a\}$, contrary to \eqref{eq:prelude-raw-cap}.
  Taking expectations in $J>m/a$ gives $\mathbb{E} J>m/a=(\lambda/a)\mathbb{E} J$, and hence $\lambda<a$.

  In particular, $q>1-x$, so $q^{k-1}/p_0>1$.
  If $\mathbb{P}(J\le m+\delta-x_0/5)>0$, then $\vartheta_{X^{\operatorname{U}}}\ge1/5$ on $\{J\le m+\delta-x_0/5\}$.
  Substituting $y=X^{\operatorname{U}}$ in \eqref{eq:prelude-tail-comparison} therefore gives
  \[
    \frac{M-X^{\operatorname{U}}}D>g(1/5)
    =\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-1/5}}5>\frac4{25}>\frac3{20}
  \]
  almost surely on $\{J\le m+\delta-x_0/5\}$, contrary to \eqref{eq:prelude-raw-cap}.
  Thus, $J>m+\delta-x_0/5$ almost surely.

  Since $0<\mathbb{E} J\le A$ and $m=\lambda\mathbb{E} J$, we have $0<m/A\le\lambda$, so $0<a-\lambda\le\eta<a$.
  Also, $D=A-m/k$ implies $D/A=1-m/(kA)\ge1-\lambda/k=q$.
  Since $x+17D/20<X^{\operatorname{U}}\le M$ almost surely, taking expectations in $0\le M-X^{\operatorname{U}}<3D/20$ completes the proof of \textup{(ii)}.

  To prove \textup{(iii)}, note that $q-(1-x)=(a-\lambda)/k$.
  Since $q\le D/A$ and $1-(a-\lambda)/(kq)=(1-x)/q>0$, we obtain
  \[
    \frac{p_0A}{Dq^{k-1}}
    =\left(1-\frac{a-\lambda}{kq}\right)^k\frac{Aq}{D}
    \le\mathrm{e}^{-(a-\lambda)/q}\le\mathrm{e}^{-(a-\lambda)}\le1.
  \]

label: cor:positive-lower-mean
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:positive-lower-mean}
    Let $k\ge6$ and $x=\beta_k$, and let $\mathsf P$ maximize $F_k$ among nonnegative Borel laws of mean at most $x$.
    Assume $0<w<W_k$, with $w=k\mathbb{E}(R_k-1)_+$ as in \cref{sec:common-bounds}.
    Use the conditional decomposition from \cref{sec:conditional-laws} with $\varepsilon=1/16$ and $\zeta=17/20$.
    Then $x_0>0$, $\lambda<a$, and $0<\eta<a$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Maximality gives $p\le p_0$.
    Together with \cref{prop:finite-shortfall-margin,prop:support-separation}, the moment identities in \cref{sec:contact}, and the bounds on $c_k$ in \cref{lem:crossing-lower-finite,lem:crossing-upper}, this verifies the hypotheses of \cref{lem:upper-intensity}.
    If $x_0=0$, then \cref{lem:upper-intensity}\textup{\ref{item:upper-intensity-zero}} gives $\mathsf P=\mathsf B_x$.
    The decomposition $\mathsf P=(1-a)\delta_0+a\mathsf Q$ then gives $\mathsf Q=(1-1/k)\delta_0+(1/k)\delta_1$, so $w=k(1-1/k)^k=W_k$, a contradiction.
    Thus $x_0>0$, and \cref{lem:upper-intensity}\textup{\ref{item:upper-intensity-parameters}} gives $\lambda<a$ and $0<\eta<a$.

label: lem:exact-upper-count
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:exact-upper-count}
  Let $k\ge6$ be an integer, $11/24\le c\le1/2$,
  $x=(k+c)^{-1}$, and $x<M\le1$.
  Suppose that $0\le\varepsilon\le1/10$ and $\zeta=17/20$.
  Let $\mathsf P$ be a probability distribution of mean $x$, supported on
  $[0,x+\varepsilon D]\cup(x+\zeta D,M]$, with
  $\mathsf P((x+\zeta D,M])>0$ and positive lower conditional mean $x_0$.
  Assume that $p\le p_0$, $D>3x$, and $r\le M$.
  For independent $X_1,\ldots,X_k$ with distribution $\mathsf P$,
  suppose that $\operatorname{Var}(X_1+\cdots+X_k)=D(r-\delta)$ and
  $\mathbb{P}(X_1+\cdots+X_{k-1}<1-y)=p(M-y)/D$ for
  $\mathsf P$-almost every $y$.
  Then the following statements hold.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item\label{item:exact-upper-count-positive} We have $0<\eta<a$ and $\mathcal V>0$.
    \item\label{item:exact-upper-count-tail} We have
    \[
      p_0\eta\le T_0
      \le\mathbb{P}\left(\frac{B_k}{A}\ge1-\eta\right).
    \]
     \end{enumerate}
     \noindent In particular, $T_0>\eta/3$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cref{lem:upper-intensity}\textup{\ref{item:upper-intensity-parameters}}, we have $\lambda<a$, $0<\eta<a$, $0<q\le D/A<1$, and $\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})\ge0$.
  We estimate the contributions to $\mathbb{P}(S_k<1)$ from samples with zero or one value in $(x+\zeta D,M]$.

  In the representation $X_i=(1-I_i)X_i^{\operatorname{L}}+I_iX_i^{\operatorname{U}}$, the probability that all $k$ samples are lower and $S_k<1$ is $q^k(1-T_0)$.
  The probability of exactly one upper sample is
  $k(1-q)q^{k-1}=\lambda q^{k-1}$.
  Conditional on $\sum_{i=1}^k I_i=1$, the sum has the distribution of $X^{\operatorname{U}}+X_1^{\operatorname{L}}+\cdots+X_{k-1}^{\operatorname{L}}$, with all variables independent.

  Since the coupling satisfies $X_i\ge X_i^{\operatorname{L}}$ almost surely, we have
  $\mathbb{P}(X_1^{\operatorname{L}}+\cdots+X_{k-1}^{\operatorname{L}}<1-y)\ge\mathbb{P}(S_{k-1}<1-y)$
  for every $y$.
  The hypothesis $\mathbb{P}(S_{k-1}<1-y)=p(M-y)/D$ holds for $\mathsf{L}(X^{\operatorname{U}})$-almost every $y$.
  Averaging over $X^{\operatorname{U}}$, independently of the lower samples, we obtain
  \[
    \mathbb{P}(X^{\operatorname{U}}+X_1^{\operatorname{L}}+\cdots+X_{k-1}^{\operatorname{L}}<1)
    \ge\frac pD\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}}).
  \]
  The event that all $k$ samples are lower and $S_k<1$ is disjoint from the event that exactly one sample is upper and $S_k<1$, so
  \[
    p\ge q^k(1-T_0)
    +\lambda q^{k-1}\frac{p\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}D.
  \]

  Since $\mathbb{E} S_k=a<1$, we have $p>0$.
  Dividing by $p$ and using $p\le p_0$ and $1-T_0\ge0$, we obtain
  \[
    \frac{q^k}{p_0}(1-T_0)
    +\frac{\lambda q^{k-1}\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}D\le1.
  \]
  Rearranging, we have
  \[
    T_0\ge1-\frac{p_0}{q^k}
    +\frac{p_0\lambda\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}{qD}.
  \]

  Since $q=1-x+(a-\lambda)/k$ and $a-\lambda>0$, the binomial
  theorem implies
  \[
    q^k-p_0\ge(a-\lambda)(1-x)^{k-1}.
  \]
  Using $q<1$, $D<A$, $(1-x)^{k-1}\ge p_0$, and
  $\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})\ge0$, we conclude that
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      T_0
       & \ge
      \frac{(a-\lambda)(1-x)^{k-1}}{q^k}
      +\frac{p_0\lambda\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}{qD}                           \\
       & \ge p_0\left(a-\lambda+\frac{\lambda\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}A\right)
      =p_0\eta.
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  The last equality uses $m=\lambda\mathbb{E} J$ and $J=A-(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})$, which give $\eta=a-\lambda+\lambda\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/A$.

  Since $\delta+m=A(1-\eta)+\delta(1-A)$, with $\delta>0$ and $A\le1$, we have $\delta+m\ge A(1-\eta)$.
  As $T_0=\mathbb{P}(B_k\ge\delta+m)$, this proves the upper bound in \textup{(ii)}.

  Since $c>0$, we have $p_0>(1-1/k)^k$.
  The sequence $(1-1/k)^k$ is increasing, and $(5/6)^6>1/3$.
  Thus $p_0>1/3$ for $k\ge6$, and hence $T_0>\eta/3$.

  Finally, if $\mathcal V=0$, then $X^{\operatorname{L}}=x_0$ almost surely.
  Since $x_0<x<1/k$, this would imply $T_0=0$,
  contradicting $T_0>\eta/3>0$.
  Therefore $\mathcal V>0$.
head: environment

label: lem:conditional-variance-bounds
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:conditional-variance-bounds}
  Let $k\ge2$ be an integer, $c>0$, $x=(k+c)^{-1}$, $x<M\le1$, and $0\le\varepsilon<\zeta<1$.
  Let $\mathsf P$ be a probability distribution of mean $x$, supported on $[0,x+\varepsilon D]\cup(x+\zeta D,M]$, with $\mathsf P((x+\zeta D,M])>0$.
  For independent $X_1,\ldots,X_k$ with distribution $\mathsf P$, assume that $\operatorname{Var}(X_1+\cdots+X_k)=D(r-\delta)$ and $\mathbb{P}(X_1+\cdots+X_{k-1}<1-y)=p(M-y)/D$ for $\mathsf P$-almost every $y$.
  Then the following statements hold.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item\label{item:conditional-variance-cap} Almost surely,
    \[
      -\frac{x_0}{A}
      \le\frac{X^{\operatorname{L}}-x_0}{A}
      \le\frac{x+\varepsilon D-x_0}{A}.
    \]
    Moreover, $\mathcal V\le kx_0(x+\varepsilon D-x_0)/A^2$.
    \item\label{item:conditional-variance-lower} We have
    \[
      \mathcal V
      \ge\frac{D}{Aq}
      \left[\frac{\eta}{a}+\frac{(1-c)x_0}{A}-\frac{M-r}{A}\right]
      +\frac{\lambda\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}{Aq}
      \left[1-(1-\zeta)\frac DA\right].
    \]
    \item\label{item:conditional-variance-small} If, in addition, $k\ge6$, $11/24\le c\le1/2$, $r\le M$, $x_0>0$, $\lambda<a$, and $J>m+\delta-x_0/5$ almost surely, then $\mathcal V<5\eta$.
  \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Subtracting $x_0$ from $0\le X^{\operatorname{L}}\le x+\varepsilon D$ and dividing by $A>0$ proves the almost-sure bounds in \textup{(i)}.
  Also, $(X^{\operatorname{L}})^2\le(x+\varepsilon D)X^{\operatorname{L}}$ almost surely.
  Taking expectations and using $\mathbb{E} X^{\operatorname{L}}=x_0$, we obtain
  $\operatorname{Var}(X^{\operatorname{L}})=\mathbb{E}[(X^{\operatorname{L}})^2]-x_0^2\le x_0(x+\varepsilon D-x_0)$.
  Thus $\mathcal V=k\operatorname{Var}(X^{\operatorname{L}})/A^2\le kx_0(x+\varepsilon D-x_0)/A^2$.

  Since $\mathsf P=q\mathsf{L}(X^{\operatorname{L}})+(1-q)\mathsf{L}(X^{\operatorname{U}})$, $\mathbb{E} X^{\operatorname{L}}=x_0$, and $J=X^{\operatorname{U}}-x_0$, we have
  $\mathbb{E}(X_1-x_0)^2=q\operatorname{Var}(X^{\operatorname{L}})+(1-q)\mathbb{E} J^2$.
  Also, $\mathbb{E}(X_1-x_0)=x-x_0=m/k$.
  By independence, $\lambda=k(1-q)$, and $A^2\mathcal V=k\operatorname{Var}(X^{\operatorname{L}})$,
  \[
    \operatorname{Var}(S_k)
    =k\mathbb{E}(X_1-x_0)^2-\frac{m^2}{k}
    =qA^2\mathcal V+\lambda\mathbb{E} J^2-\frac{m^2}{k}.
  \]

  Write $\Theta=\lambda\mathbb{E}[(J/A)(1-J/A)]$.
  Since $\lambda\mathbb{E} J=m$, we have
  $\lambda\mathbb{E} J^2/A^2=m/A-\Theta$.
  Substituting $\operatorname{Var}(S_k)=D(r-\delta)$ and
  $\lambda\mathbb{E} J^2/A^2=m/A-\Theta$, we obtain
  $q\mathcal V=D(r-\delta)/A^2-m/A+m^2/(kA^2)+\Theta$.
  Since $M=A+x_0$ and $\delta=cx_0+cm/k$, we have
  $(r-\delta)/A=1+(1-c)x_0/A-cm/(kA)-(M-r)/A$.
  Also, $m/A-m^2/(kA^2)=Dm/A^2$, since $D=A-m/k$.
  Consequently,
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:normalized-variance-identity}
    \begin{aligned}
      q\mathcal V
       & =\frac DA\left[\eta+\frac{(1-c)x_0}{A}
      +\frac{c\eta}{k}-\frac{M-r}{A}\right]+\Theta        \\
       & =\frac DA\left[\frac{\eta}{a}+\frac{(1-c)x_0}{A}
        -\frac{M-r}{A}\right]+\Theta.
    \end{aligned}
  \end{equation}
  Here $1-(m/A)(1+c/k)=\eta(1+c/k)=\eta/a$, because
  $\eta=a-m/A$ and $a^{-1}=1+c/k$.

  Since $x+\zeta D<X^{\operatorname{U}}\le M$, we have
  $1-(1-\zeta)D/A<J/A\le1$.
  Multiplying $J/A>1-(1-\zeta)D/A$ by
  $\lambda(1-J/A)\ge0$ and taking expectations, we obtain
  \[
    \Theta
    \ge\lambda\left[1-(1-\zeta)\frac DA\right]\mathbb{E}(1-J/A)
    =\frac{\lambda\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}A\left[1-(1-\zeta)\frac DA\right].
  \]
  The equality follows from $1-J/A=(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/A$.
  Substituting
  $\Theta\ge\lambda\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})[1-(1-\zeta)D/A]/A$
  into \eqref{eq:normalized-variance-identity} and dividing by
  $q>0$ proves the lower bound for $\mathcal V$.

  We now prove $\mathcal V<5\eta$.
  Assume that $k\ge6$, $11/24\le c\le1/2$, $r\le M$,
  $x_0>0$, $\lambda<a$, and
  $J>m+\delta-x_0/5$ almost surely.
  Taking expectations in $J>m+\delta-x_0/5$ and using
  $m=\lambda\mathbb{E} J$, we obtain
  $(1-\lambda)\mathbb{E} J-\delta>-x_0/5$.
  Since $kx_0=a-\lambda\mathbb{E} J$, we have
  \[
    \frac{(a-\lambda)\mathbb{E} J}{a}-cx_0
    =(1-\lambda)\mathbb{E} J-\delta
    >-\frac{x_0}{5}.
  \]
  Hence $(a-\lambda)\mathbb{E} J>a(c-1/5)x_0$.
  Since $a-\lambda>0$ and $\mathbb{E} J\le A$, it follows that
  $x_0/A<(a-\lambda)/[a(c-1/5)]$.
  Moreover, $0<m/A=\lambda\mathbb{E} J/A\le\lambda<a$ implies
  $0<a-\lambda\le\eta<a$.

  Since $(J-A)^2\ge0$, we have $J^2\ge2AJ-A^2$.
  Taking expectations and using $\lambda\mathbb{E} J=m$, we obtain
  $\lambda\mathbb{E} J^2/A^2\ge2m/A-\lambda$.
  Therefore,
  $\Theta=m/A-\lambda\mathbb{E} J^2/A^2\le\lambda-m/A=\eta-(a-\lambda)$.
  Since $M-r\ge0$, $D/A\le1$, $\eta>0$, and $1-c>0$,
  \eqref{eq:normalized-variance-identity} implies
  \[
    q\mathcal V
    \le\left(2+\frac ck\right)\eta-(a-\lambda)+\frac{(1-c)x_0}{A}.
  \]

  For $11/24\le c\le1/2$ and $a<1$, we have
  $(1-c)/[a(c-1/5)]-1>0$.
  Substituting $x_0/A<(a-\lambda)/[a(c-1/5)]$ and then
  using $a-\lambda\le\eta$, we obtain
  \[
    \mathcal V
    <\frac{1+(1-c)/[a(c-1/5)]+c/k}{q}\eta.
  \]
  Since $k\ge6$ and $11/24\le c\le1/2$, we have
  $a\ge12/13$, $(1-c)/[a(c-1/5)]<5/2$, and $c/k\le1/12$.
  Also, $\lambda<a<1$ implies $q=1-\lambda/k>5/6$.
  Since $(6/5)(1+5/2+1/12)<5$, we conclude that $\mathcal V<5\eta$.

label: lem:averaged-contact-normal
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:averaged-contact-normal}
  Let $k\ge6$ be an integer, $11/24\le c\le1/2$, $x=(k+c)^{-1}$, and $x<M\le1$.
  Suppose that $0\le\varepsilon\le1/10$ and $\zeta=17/20$.
  Let $\mathsf P$ be a probability distribution of mean $x$, supported on $[0,x+\varepsilon D]\cup(x+\zeta D,M]$, with $\mathsf P((x+\zeta D,M])>0$ and positive lower conditional mean $x_0$.
  Assume that $p\le p_0$, $D>3x$, and $r\le M$.
  For independent $X_1,\ldots,X_k$ with distribution $\mathsf P$, suppose that $\operatorname{Var}(X_1+\cdots+X_k)=D(r-\delta)$ and $\mathbb{P}(X_1+\cdots+X_{k-1}<1-y)=p(M-y)/D$ for $\mathsf P$-almost every $y$.
  If $B_*>0$ and $|X^{\operatorname{L}}-x_0|\le AB_*$ almost surely, then
  \[
    \left(\frac12-\frac{p_0\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}{Dq^{k-1}}\right)
    \sqrt{\frac{k-1}{k}\mathcal V}
    \le\frac25Q+\frac{B_*}{3}
    +\frac17\sqrt{\frac{\mathcal V}{k}}.
  \]
  Moreover, $Q<\eta/a-\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/A-(c-1/5)x_0/A$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Take $X^{\operatorname{U}}$ independently of $X_1^{\operatorname{L}},\ldots,X_{k-1}^{\operatorname{L}}$.
  We first estimate $\mathbb{P}(B_{k-1}+J<\delta+m)$ from above.
  In the representation $X_i=(1-I_i)X_i^{\operatorname{L}}+I_iX_i^{\operatorname{U}}$, the event that all $k-1$ observations are lower has probability $q^{k-1}$.
  Conditional on $I_1=\cdots=I_{k-1}=0$, their sum has the distribution of $X_1^{\operatorname{L}}+\cdots+X_{k-1}^{\operatorname{L}}$.
    {Thus, for each fixed $y$, the probability that all $k-1$ observations are lower and their sum is less than $1-y$ is at most $\mathbb{P}(S_{k-1}<1-y)$.}
  The hypothesis $\mathbb{P}(S_{k-1}<1-y)=p(M-y)/D$ holds for $\mathsf{L}(X^{\operatorname{U}})$-almost every $y$.
  Consequently,
  \[
    q^{k-1}\mathbb{P}(X_1^{\operatorname{L}}+\cdots+X_{k-1}^{\operatorname{L}}<1-y)
    \le p\frac{M-y}{D}.
  \]

  Since $X^{\operatorname{U}}=x_0+J$ and $1-kx_0=\delta+m$, the event $X^{\operatorname{U}}+X_1^{\operatorname{L}}+\cdots+X_{k-1}^{\operatorname{L}}<1$ is equivalent to $B_{k-1}+J<\delta+m$.
  Dividing the preceding inequality by $q^{k-1}$ and averaging over $X^{\operatorname{U}}$, we obtain
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:conditional-failure-average}
    \mathbb{P}(B_{k-1}+J<\delta+m)
    \le\frac{p\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}{Dq^{k-1}}
    \le\frac{p_0\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}{Dq^{k-1}}.
  \end{equation}
  The last inequality follows from $p\le p_0$ and $\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})\ge0$.

  We now estimate the same probability from below.
  By \cref{lem:exact-upper-count}\textup{\ref{item:exact-upper-count-positive}}, we have $\mathcal V>0$.
  Write $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(B_{k-1}/A)=(k-1)\mathcal V/k$.
  {The variables $(X_i^{\operatorname{L}}-x_0)/A$} are independent, identically distributed, and have mean zero.
  Since their absolute values are at most $B_*$, we have
  \[
    (k-1)\mathbb{E}\left|\frac{X^{\operatorname{L}}-x_0}{A}\right|^3
    \le B_*(k-1)\mathbb{E}\left(\frac{X^{\operatorname{L}}-x_0}{A}\right)^2
    =B_*\sigma^2.
  \]
  By \cref{lem:normal-comparison}, the absolute difference between $\mathbb{P}(B_{k-1}/A<s)$ and $\Phi(s/\sigma)$ is at most $B_*/(3\sigma)+1/(7\sqrt{k-1})$ for every real $s$.
  Here $\Phi$ denotes the standard normal distribution function.

  Since $J$ is independent of the lower observations, conditioning on $J$ does not change the distribution of $B_{k-1}/A$.
  We may therefore apply this inequality at $s=(\delta+m-J)/A$ and then take expectations over $J$.
    {To estimate $\mathbb{E}\Phi((\delta+m-J)/(A\sigma))$, note that} $\Phi(-t)\ge1/2-(2/5)t_+$ for every real $t$, since $\Phi'(u)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\mathrm{e}^{-u^2/2}<2/5$ for every $u\in\mathbb R$.
  Applying this inequality with $t=(J-m-\delta)/(A\sigma)$ and using the definition of $Q$, we obtain $\mathbb{E}\Phi((\delta+m-J)/(A\sigma))\ge1/2-2Q/(5\sigma)$.
  Together with \eqref{eq:conditional-failure-average}, these estimates imply
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      \frac{p_0\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}{Dq^{k-1}}
       & \ge
      \mathbb{E}\Phi\left(\frac{\delta+m-J}{A\sigma}\right)
      -\frac{B_*}{3\sigma}-\frac1{7\sqrt{k-1}} \\
       & \ge
      \frac12-\frac{2Q}{5\sigma}
      -\frac{B_*}{3\sigma}-\frac1{7\sqrt{k-1}}.
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  Rearranging and multiplying by $\sigma>0$ proves the first assertion, since $\sigma=\sqrt{(k-1)\mathcal V/k}$ and $\sigma/\sqrt{k-1}=\sqrt{\mathcal V/k}$.

  It remains to prove $Q<\eta/a-\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/A-(c-1/5)x_0/A$.
  We first compute $\mathbb{E}(J-m-\delta)$, and then estimate the contribution from the event $J<m+\delta$.
  Since $x=x_0+m/k$ and $\delta=cx$, we have $\delta/A=cx_0/A+cm/(kA)$.
  Using $\mathbb{E} J=A-\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})$, $a^{-1}=1+c/k$, and $\eta=a-m/A$, we obtain
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      \frac{\mathbb{E}(J-m-\delta)}A
       & =1-\frac{\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}A-\frac mA-\frac{\delta}{A}      \\
       & =1-\frac{\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}A-\frac{cx_0}{A}
      -\frac mA\left(1+\frac ck\right)                                        \\
       & =\frac{\eta}{a}-\frac{\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}A-\frac{cx_0}{A}.
    \end{aligned}
  \]

  By \cref{lem:upper-intensity}\textup{\ref{item:upper-intensity-parameters}}, we have $J>m+\delta-x_0/5$ almost surely.
  Since $x_0>0$, it follows that $(m+\delta-J)_+<x_0/5$ almost surely, and hence $\mathbb{E}(m+\delta-J)_+<x_0/5$.
  Applying the identity $s_+=s+(-s)_+$ to $s=J-m-\delta$ and taking expectations, we conclude that
  \[
    Q
    =\frac{\mathbb{E}(J-m-\delta)}A
    +\frac{\mathbb{E}(m+\delta-J)_+}{A}
    <\frac{\eta}{a}-\frac{\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}A-\left(c-\frac15\right)\frac{x_0}{A}.
  \]
head: environment

label: lem:large-defect
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:large-defect}
  Let $k\ge6$ be an integer, $11/24\le c\le1/2$, $x=(k+c)^{-1}$, and $x<M\le1$.
  Set $D=M-x$, $\varepsilon=1/16$, and $\zeta=17/20$.
  Suppose that $\mathsf P$ is a probability distribution of mean $x$ such that
  \[
    \mathsf P\bigl([0,x+D/16]\cup(x+17D/20,M]\bigr)=1
    \text{ and }\mathsf P((x+17D/20,M])>0.
  \]
  Suppose also that $x_0>0$.
  Assume that $p\le p_0$, $D>3x$, $r\le M$, and $(M-r)/D<1/20-3x/(20D)$, and that $\operatorname{Var}(S_k)=D(r-\delta)$ and $\mathbb{P}(S_{k-1}<1-y)=p(M-y)/D$ for $\mathsf P$-almost every $y$.
  Then $\eta/a<1/10$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $\eta/a\ge1/10$, and set $t=1/k$ and $\rho=3/20$.
  By \cref{lem:upper-intensity}\textup{\ref{item:upper-intensity-parameters}} and the assumptions on $k$ and $c$, we have $0<t\le1/6$, $1/10\le\eta/a<1$, and $12/13\le a<1$.
  Also, $x_0<x$ and $A>D>3x$ imply $0<x_0/A<1/3$.
  We have $m/A=a(1-\eta/a)$ and $D/A=1-tm/A$.
  Set $\theta=\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/(\rho D)$.
  Since $0\le M-X^{\operatorname{U}}<\rho D$ almost surely, we have $0\le\theta<1$.
  Also, $(x+D/16-x_0)/A=1/16+15tm/(16A)$.

  We will derive
  \[
    (1-\theta)P_0(t,\eta/a,x_0/A)
    +\theta P_1(t,\eta/a,x_0/A)<0,
  \]
  where $P_0$ and $P_1$ will be defined in \eqref{eq:large-defect-endpoint-functions}.
  However, \cref{clm:large-defect-endpoint-positive} gives $P_0(t,\eta/a,x_0/A)>0$ and $P_1(t,\eta/a,x_0/A)>0$.
  Since $0\le\theta<1$, their weighted sum is positive, a contradiction.

  To estimate $\mathcal V$ from below, set
  \[
    \mathcal V_0=\frac{\eta}{a}-\frac1{20}+\frac{13x_0}{20A}
    +\frac{t(1-\eta/a)}6,
    \text{ and }\mathcal V_1=\mathcal V_0+\frac{1-\eta/a}{9}.
  \]
  We have $\mathcal V_1\ge \mathcal V_0\ge1/20$.
  Since $x/A=x_0/A+tm/A$ and $D/A=1-tm/A$, the assumption $(M-r)/D<1/20-3x/(20D)$ implies
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      \frac{\eta}{a}+\frac{(1-c)x_0}{A}-\frac{M-r}{A}
       & >\frac{\eta}{a}-\frac1{20}
      +\left(1-c+\frac3{20}\right)\frac{x_0}{A}
      +\frac{tm}{5A}                  \\
       & =\frac{\eta}{a}-\frac1{20}
      +\left(1-c+\frac3{20}\right)\frac{x_0}{A}
      +\frac{at(1-\eta/a)}5
      \ge \mathcal V_0.
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  The last inequality uses $c\le1/2$ and $a/5\ge12/65>1/6$.
  Using $q\le D/A$, $\lambda\ge m/A$, and $\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})=\theta\rho D$ in \cref{lem:conditional-variance-bounds}\textup{\ref{item:conditional-variance-lower}}, we obtain
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:large-defect-variance-lower}
    \begin{aligned}
      \mathcal V
       & >\frac{D\mathcal V_0}{Aq}
      +\frac{\lambda\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}{Aq}\left(1-\frac{\rho D}{A}\right) \\
       & \ge \mathcal V_0+\rho(1-\rho)\frac mA\theta
      \ge(1-\theta)\mathcal V_0+\theta \mathcal V_1.
    \end{aligned}
  \end{equation}
  The last inequality follows from $m/A=a(1-\eta/a)$ and $\rho(1-\rho)a>1/9$.

  We next estimate $Q$ in \cref{lem:averaged-contact-normal}.
  We have $0\le(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/A<\rho D/A$, $\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/A=\theta\rho D/A$, and $Q=\mathbb{E}(\eta/a-cx_0/A-(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/A)_+$.
  Set $Q_0=(\eta/a-11x_0/(24A))_+$ and $Q_1=(\eta/a-11x_0/(24A)-\rho+\rho t(1-\eta/a))_+$.
  By convexity of $s\mapsto(\eta/a-cx_0/A-s)_+$ on $[0,\rho D/A]$ and the equality $\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/(\rho D)=\theta$, we obtain
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      Q & \le(1-\theta)\left(\frac{\eta}{a}-\frac{cx_0}{A}\right)_+
      +\theta\left(\frac{\eta}{a}-\frac{cx_0}{A}-\frac{\rho D}{A}\right)_+ \\
        & \le(1-\theta)Q_0+\theta Q_1.
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  The second inequality uses $c\ge11/24$ and $\rho D/A\ge\rho-\rho t(1-\eta/a)$.

  To bound $B_*/3+(1/7)\sqrt{\mathcal V/k}$ in \cref{lem:averaged-contact-normal}, write
  \[
    E=\frac1{16}+\frac{15t(1-\eta/a)}{16},
    \text{ and }R=\frac{\max\{x_0/A,E\}}3+\frac{x_0/A+E}{14}.
  \]
  By \cref{lem:conditional-variance-bounds}\textup{\ref{item:conditional-variance-cap}}, we may take $B_*=\max\{x_0/A,(x+D/16-x_0)/A\}$ in \cref{lem:averaged-contact-normal}.
  We have $(x+D/16-x_0)/A\le E$, and $\mathcal V\le kx_0(x+D/16-x_0)/A^2$ by \cref{lem:conditional-variance-bounds}\textup{\ref{item:conditional-variance-cap}}.
  The arithmetic--geometric mean inequality therefore yields
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      \frac{B_*}{3}+\frac17\sqrt{\frac{\mathcal V}{k}}
       & \le\frac{\max\{x_0/A,E\}}3
      +\frac{\sqrt{x_0(x+D/16-x_0)}}{7A} \\
       & \le\frac{\max\{x_0/A,E\}}3
      +\frac17\sqrt{\frac{x_0}{A}E}      \\
       & \le\frac{\max\{x_0/A,E\}}3
      +\frac{x_0/A+E}{14}=R.
    \end{aligned}
  \]

  Define $\beta(s)=\sqrt{(1+s)/11}$ for $1/10\le s\le1$.
  We will prove
  \[
    \frac12-\rho\frac{p_0A}{Dq^{k-1}}>\beta(\eta/a).
  \]
  By \cref{lem:upper-intensity}\textup{\ref{item:upper-intensity-ratio}}, $p_0A/(Dq^{k-1})\le\mathrm{e}^{-(a-\lambda)}\le1$.
  Since $a\ge12/13$ and
  \[
    \mathrm{e}^{12/13}
    >1+\frac{12}{13}+\frac12\left(\frac{12}{13}\right)^2
    =\frac{397}{169}>\frac94,
  \]
  we have $\mathrm{e}^{-a}<4/9$.
  Convexity of $z\mapsto\mathrm{e}^{-z}$ on $[0,a]$ and $0<a-\lambda<a$ give
  \[
    \frac{p_0A}{Dq^{k-1}}
    \le\mathrm{e}^{-(a-\lambda)}
    \le1-(1-\mathrm{e}^{-a})\frac{a-\lambda}{a}
    <1-\frac{5(a-\lambda)}{9a}.
  \]
  Since $m=\lambda\mathbb{E} J$, $J=A-(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})$, and $\eta=a-m/A$, we have
  \[
    \frac{a-\lambda}{a}
    =\frac{\eta/a-\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/A}{1-\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/A}.
  \]
  If $\eta/a\ge\rho$, then $\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/A<\rho$ implies $(a-\lambda)/a\ge(\eta/a-\rho)/(1-\rho)$, and hence
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      \frac12-\rho\frac{p_0A}{Dq^{k-1}}
       & \ge\frac7{20}+\frac5{51}\left(\frac{\eta}{a}-\frac3{20}\right) \\
       & =\frac13+\frac{\eta}{10a}+\frac{1-\eta/a}{510}
      \ge\frac13+\frac{\eta}{10a}.
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  If $\eta/a\le\rho$, then $p_0A/(Dq^{k-1})\le1$ gives $1/2-\rho p_0A/(Dq^{k-1})\ge7/20>1/3+\eta/(10a)$.
  For $1/10\le s\le1$, the arithmetic--geometric mean inequality and $\sqrt{2/11}<13/30$ give
  \[
    \beta(s)
    =\sqrt{\frac2{11}}\sqrt{\frac{1+s}{2}}
    \le\sqrt{\frac2{11}}\frac{3+s}{4}
    <\frac{13(3+s)}{120}
    \le\frac13+\frac{s}{10}.
  \]
  The last inequality is equivalent to $s\le1$.
  Thus, $1/2-\rho p_0A/(Dq^{k-1})>\beta(\eta/a)$, and $0<\beta(s)<1/2$ for $1/10\le s\le1$.
  Since $\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})=\rho D\theta$ and $D/A<1$, we obtain
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      \frac12-\frac{p_0\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}{Dq^{k-1}}
       & =\frac12-\rho\theta\frac DA\frac{p_0A}{Dq^{k-1}} \\
       & \ge\frac{1-\theta}{2}
      +\theta\left(\frac12-\rho\frac{p_0A}{Dq^{k-1}}\right)
      \ge\frac{1-\theta}{2}+\theta\beta(\eta/a)>0.
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  We may therefore substitute \eqref{eq:large-defect-variance-lower} into the left-hand side of the inequality in \cref{lem:averaged-contact-normal}.
  Using also $Q\le(1-\theta)Q_0+\theta Q_1$ and $B_*/3+(1/7)\sqrt{\mathcal V/k}\le R$, we obtain
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:large-defect-normal}
    \begin{aligned}
       & \left(\frac{1-\theta}{2}+\theta\beta(\eta/a)\right)
      \sqrt{(1-t)\bigl((1-\theta)\mathcal V_0+\theta \mathcal V_1\bigr)} \\
       & \qquad<\frac25\bigl((1-\theta)Q_0+\theta Q_1\bigr)+R.
    \end{aligned}
  \end{equation}
  Define
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:large-defect-endpoint-functions}
    \begin{aligned}
      P_0(t,\eta/a,x_0/A)
       & =\frac12\sqrt{(1-t)\mathcal V_0}-\frac25Q_0-R,         \\
      P_1(t,\eta/a,x_0/A)
       & =\beta(\eta/a)\sqrt{(1-t)\mathcal V_1}-\frac25Q_1-R.
    \end{aligned}
  \end{equation}
  Since $0<\beta(\eta/a)<1/2$ and $\mathcal V_1\ge \mathcal V_0$, concavity of the square root gives
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
       & \left(\frac{1-\theta}{2}+\theta\beta(\eta/a)\right)
      \sqrt{(1-\theta)\mathcal V_0+\theta \mathcal V_1}                   \\
       & \quad\ge\left(\frac{1-\theta}{2}+\theta\beta(\eta/a)\right)
      \bigl((1-\theta)\sqrt{\mathcal V_0}+\theta\sqrt{\mathcal V_1}\bigr) \\
       & \quad=\frac{1-\theta}{2}\sqrt{\mathcal V_0}
      +\theta\beta(\eta/a)\sqrt{\mathcal V_1}                           \\
       & \qquad\quad+\theta(1-\theta)\bigl(1/2-\beta(\eta/a)\bigr)
      \bigl(\sqrt{\mathcal V_1}-\sqrt{\mathcal V_0}\bigr)                 \\
       & \quad\ge\frac{1-\theta}{2}\sqrt{\mathcal V_0}
      +\theta\beta(\eta/a)\sqrt{\mathcal V_1}.
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  After multiplication by $\sqrt{1-t}$, \eqref{eq:large-defect-normal} yields
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:large-defect-contact-obstruction}
    (1-\theta)P_0(t,\eta/a,x_0/A)
    +\theta P_1(t,\eta/a,x_0/A)<0.
  \end{equation}
  We extend the defining formulas for $P_0,P_1$ and their auxiliary functions by allowing $t$, $\eta/a$, and $x_0/A$ to vary independently over $[0,1/6]\times[1/10,1]\times[0,1/3]$.
  \begin{claim}\label{clm:large-defect-endpoint-positive}
    The functions $P_0$ and $P_1$ defined in \eqref{eq:large-defect-endpoint-functions} are positive throughout $[0,1/6]\times[1/10,1]\times[0,1/3]$.
  \end{claim}
  The proof of \cref{clm:large-defect-endpoint-positive} is given in \cref{app:large-defect-endpoint-positive}.
  Since $0\le\theta<1$, \cref{clm:large-defect-endpoint-positive} contradicts \eqref{eq:large-defect-contact-obstruction}.
  Therefore, $\eta/a<1/10$.

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cref{cor:positive-lower-mean}, we have $x_0>0$ and $\eta>0$.
    The moment identities in \cref{sec:contact}, \cref{prop:finite-shortfall-margin,prop:support-separation}, and the bounds on $c_k$ verify the remaining hypotheses of \cref{lem:large-defect}.
    Hence $\eta/a<1/10$.
    Since $a=k/(k+c_k)<1$, we obtain $0<\eta<a/10<1/10$.

label: lem:conditional-support
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:conditional-support}
    Let $k\ge6$ be an integer, $11/24\le c\le1/2$, $x=(k+c)^{-1}$, $x<M\le1$, and $0\le\varepsilon\le1/10$, and set $D=M-x$ and $\zeta=17/20$.
    Let $\mathsf P$ be a probability law of mean $x$, supported on $[0,x+\varepsilon D]\cup(x+17D/20,M]$, with positive mass on the upper interval.
    Use the conditional notation from \cref{sec:conditional-laws}, and set $\mathcal V=k\operatorname{Var}(X^{\operatorname{L}})/A^2$.
    For independent $X_1,\ldots,X_k$ with law $\mathsf P$, write $h(t)=\mathbb{P}(S_{k-1}+t\ge1)$.
    Assume that $p\le p_0$, $0\le M-r<(D-3x)/20$, and $h(y)-h(0)=py/D$ for $\mathsf P$-almost every $y$.
    If $0<\eta\le1/10$, then $ess sup X^{\operatorname{L}}<A/10$ and $\mathcal V<1/25$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The assumption $0\le M-r<(D-3x)/20$ implies $r\le M$ and $D>3x$.
  Also, $x_0>0$: otherwise $m=a$ and $A=M\le1$, so $\eta=a-a/M\le0$, contrary to $\eta>0$.
  Taking expectations in $h(X_1)-h(0)=pX_1/D$ gives
  \[
    1-p-h(0)=\mathbb{E}[h(X_1)-h(0)]=\frac{px}{D}.
  \]
  Since $D+x=M$, it follows that
  \[
    1-h(0)=\frac{pM}{D},\text{ and }
    \mathbb{P}(S_{k-1}<1-y)=\frac{p(M-y)}D
    \quad\text{for $\mathsf P$-almost every $y$.}
  \]
    The contact identity gives, for every bounded Borel function $\varphi$,
    \[
      \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_1)\mid S_k<1]
      =\frac{\mathbb{E}[(M-X_1)\varphi(X_1)]}{D}.
    \]
    Taking $\varphi(y)=y$ and using $\mathbb{E}[X_1\mid S_k<1]=(1-r)/k$ yields $\operatorname{Var}(S_k)=D(r-\delta)$.
    Write $v=\operatorname{Var}(S_k\mid S_k<1)$, and let $X,X'$ be independent with law $\mathsf P$.
    The covariance calculation in the proof of \cref{lem:contact-moment} uses only independence and these identities, and therefore yields
    \[
      v=(r-\delta)(M-r)
      -\frac{k}{2p}\mathbb{E}\left[(X-X')\int_{X'}^X(h(t)-h(0))\,\mathrm{d} t\right].
    \]
  Applying \cref{lem:upper-intensity}\textup{\ref{item:upper-intensity-parameters}}, we obtain $\lambda<a<1$ and $0\le\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/A<3/20$.
  Since $k\ge6$, $a\ge12/13$, and $\eta\le1/10$, we have $q=1-\lambda/k>5/6$ and $m/A=a-\eta\ge12/13-1/10>4/5$.
  Since $x=qx_0+(1-q)\mathbb{E} X^{\operatorname{U}}$, we also have $\lambda(\mathbb{E} X^{\operatorname{U}}-x_0)=m$.

  Set $b_0=ess sup X^{\operatorname{L}}\ge x_0>0$.
  Since $v\ge0$, we have
  \[
    \frac{k}{2p}\mathbb{E}\left[
      (X-X')\int_{X'}^X\bigl(h(t)-h(0)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d} t
      \right]\le(r-\delta)(M-r).
  \]
  We will prove $\frac12Ab_0<(r-\delta)(M-r)<A^2/20$, and hence $b_0<A/10$.
  Since $D<A$ and $x_0<x$, we have
  \[
    0\le M-r<\frac{D-3x}{20}<\frac{A-3x_0}{20}.
  \]
  Consequently, $A>3x_0$.
  Since $r-\delta=\operatorname{Var}(S_k)/D\ge0$ and $r-\delta\le M=A+x_0$, we have
  \[
    (r-\delta)(M-r)
    <\frac{(A+x_0)(A-3x_0)}{20}<\frac{A^2}{20}.
  \]

  For each integer $n\ge1$, choose $y_n\in[0,x+\varepsilon D]\cap(b_0-1/n,b_0]$ such that $h(y_n)-h(0)=py_n/D$.
  Such a choice is possible because $\mathbb{P}(X^{\operatorname{L}}>b_0-1/n)>0$ and $h(y)-h(0)=py/D$ for almost every $y$ under the law of $X^{\operatorname{L}}$.
  For every $t>b_0$, monotonicity gives $h(t)-h(0)\ge py_n/D$ for all $n$, and letting $n\to\infty$ yields $h(t)-h(0)\ge pb_0/D$.
  Since $h(t)-h(0)\ge0$ for $t\ge0$, independent variables $X^{\operatorname{L}}$ and $X^{\operatorname{U}}$ satisfy
  \[
    \int_{X^{\operatorname{L}}}^{X^{\operatorname{U}}}(h(t)-h(0))\,\mathrm{d} t\ge\frac{pb_0}{D}(X^{\operatorname{U}}-b_0),
    \text{ and }
    X^{\operatorname{U}}-b_0>\left(\frac{17}{20}-\varepsilon\right)D
    \ge\frac{3D}{4}.
  \]
  The product $(X-X')\int_{X'}^X(h(t)-h(0))\,\mathrm{d} t$ is nonnegative and unchanged when $X$ and $X'$ are interchanged.
  We retain only the pairs satisfying $X\in[0,x+\varepsilon D]$ and $X'\in(x+17D/20,M]$, together with the pairs satisfying the reversed conditions.
  The two events have total probability $2q(1-q)$.
  Using $\lambda=k(1-q)$, $\mathbb{E}(X^{\operatorname{U}}-X^{\operatorname{L}})=\mathbb{E} X^{\operatorname{U}}-x_0$, and $\lambda(\mathbb{E} X^{\operatorname{U}}-x_0)=m$, we obtain
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      \frac12Ab_0
       & <\frac34mqb_0
      <\frac{\lambda qb_0}{D}\mathbb{E}[(X^{\operatorname{U}}-X^{\operatorname{L}})(X^{\operatorname{U}}-b_0)] \\
       & \le(r-\delta)(M-r)<\frac{A^2}{20}.
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  The first inequality uses $m/A>4/5$ and $q>5/6$, and the second uses $X^{\operatorname{U}}-b_0>3D/4$.
  Thus, $b_0<A/10$.

  To prove $\mathcal V<1/25$, we apply \cref{lem:averaged-contact-normal} with $B_*=1/10$, since $0\le X^{\operatorname{L}},x_0\le b_0<A/10$.
  In particular, $Q<\eta/a-\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/A-(c-1/5)x_0/A<\eta/a-\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/A\le13/120-\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/A$.
  By \cref{lem:upper-intensity}\textup{\ref{item:upper-intensity-ratio}}, we have $p_0A/(Dq^{k-1})\le1$, so $p_0\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/(Dq^{k-1})\le\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/A$.
  Using $\sqrt{(k-1)/k}>9/10$ and $1/(7\sqrt{k})<3/50$ in \cref{lem:averaged-contact-normal}, we obtain
  \[
    \frac9{10}\left(\frac12-\frac{\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}A\right)\sqrt{\mathcal V}
    <\frac25\left(\frac{13}{120}-\frac{\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}A\right)
    +\frac1{30}+\frac3{50}\sqrt{\mathcal V}.
  \]
  Rearranging gives
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:small-defect-variance-comparison}
    \begin{aligned}
      \left(\frac{39}{100}-\frac{9\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}{10A}\right)\sqrt{\mathcal V}
       & <\frac{23}{300}-\frac{2\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}{5A}                       \\
       & <\frac15\left(\frac{39}{100}-\frac{9\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})}{10A}\right).
    \end{aligned}
  \end{equation}
  The second inequality follows because the difference between its right- and left-hand sides is $1/750+11\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/(50A)>0$.
  As $\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/A<3/20$, the coefficient $39/100-9\mathbb{E}(M-X^{\operatorname{U}})/(10A)$ is positive.
  Dividing \eqref{eq:small-defect-variance-comparison} by this coefficient yields $\sqrt{\mathcal V}<1/5$, and hence $\mathcal V<1/25$.

label: lem:small-conditional-tail
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:small-conditional-tail}
  Let $k\ge1$ be an integer and $0<\eta\le1/10$.
  Suppose that $V_1,\ldots,V_k$ are independent random variables satisfying $\mathbb{E} V_i=0$ and $|V_i|\le1/10$ almost surely for every $i$.
  If $\sum_{i=1}^k\operatorname{Var}(V_i)<\min\{5\eta,1/25\}$, then $\mathbb{P}(V_1+\cdots+V_k\ge1-\eta)<\eta/3$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $S=\sum_{i=1}^kV_i$, $v=\sum_{i=1}^k\mathbb{E} V_i^2$, and $\psi(t)=\mathrm{e}^t-1-t$.
  We prove $\mathbb{P}(S\ge1-\eta)\le v/16$, which gives the result because $v/16<5\eta/16<\eta/3$.
  We will apply Markov's inequality to $\psi(10S)$.
  Since $\mathbb{E} S=0$, we have $\mathbb{E}\psi(10S)=\mathbb{E}\mathrm{e}^{10S}-1$.
  Taylor's formula gives, for $|t|\le1$,
  \[
    0\le\psi(t)
    =t^2\int_0^1(1-s)\mathrm{e}^{st}\,\mathrm{d} s
    \le\frac34t^2,
  \]
  since $\int_0^1(1-s)\mathrm{e}^s\,\mathrm{d} s=\mathrm{e}-2<3/4$.
  Thus, $\mathbb{E}\mathrm{e}^{10V_i}\le1+75\mathbb{E} V_i^2$.
  By independence,
  \[
    \mathbb{E}\mathrm{e}^{10S}
    \le\prod_{i=1}^k(1+75\mathbb{E} V_i^2)\le\mathrm{e}^{75v}.
  \]
  Since the function $s\mapsto\mathrm{e}^{75s}-1$ is convex and $0\le v<1/25$, we obtain
  \[
    \mathbb{E}\psi(10S)=\mathbb{E}\mathrm{e}^{10S}-1
    \le\mathrm{e}^{75v}-1\le25v(\mathrm{e}^3-1).
  \]
  The function $\psi$ is nonnegative on $\mathbb R$ and increasing on $[0,\infty)$.
  As $1-\eta\ge9/10$, the event $S\ge1-\eta$ implies $\psi(10S)\ge\psi(9)$.
  Markov's inequality therefore yields
  \[
    \mathbb{P}(S\ge1-\eta)
    \le\frac{\mathbb{E}\psi(10S)}{\psi(9)}
    \le25v\frac{\mathrm{e}^3-1}{\mathrm{e}^9-10}
    \le\frac v{16}<\frac{5\eta}{16}<\frac{\eta}{3}.
  \]
  The numerical bound $(\mathrm{e}^3-1)/(\mathrm{e}^9-10)<\mathrm{e}^{-6}<1/400$ follows from $\mathrm{e}^3>20$.
head: environment

label: prop:maximizing-endpoints
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:maximizing-endpoints}
  Let $k\ge2$ and $x=\beta_k$.
  Suppose that $\mathsf P$ maximizes $F_k$ among nonnegative Borel probability laws of mean at most $x$.
  Write $\mathsf P=(1-a)\delta_0+a\mathsf Q$ as in \cref{prop:normalization}, where $a=kx$.
  For independent $Y_1,\ldots,Y_k$ with law $\mathsf Q$, set $w=k\mathbb{E}(Y_1+\cdots+Y_k-1)_+$.
  Then $w=0$ or $w=W_k$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $2\le k\le5$, the conclusion follows from \cref{lem:initial-nodes}\textup{(iv)}.
  Fix $k\ge6$ and write $x=\beta_k=(k+c_k)^{-1}$.
  Let $\mathsf P$ be any maximizing distribution under the constraint $m(\mathsf P)\le x$.
  By \cref{prop:normalization}, $\mathsf P$ is supported on $[0,1]$, has mean $x$, and can be written as
  \[
    \mathsf P=(1-a)\delta_0+a\mathsf Q,
  \]
  where $a=kx$ and $\mathsf Q\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])$ has mean $1/k$.
  In particular, $\mathsf P(\{0\})\ge1-a>0$.
  For independent $X_1,\ldots,X_k$ with law $\mathsf P$, we retain the notation $S_j,p,h,r$ from \cref{sec:contact}.
  Since $\mathbb{E} S_k=a<1$, we have $p>0$.
  Both $\mathsf B_x$ and $\mathsf C_{k,x}$ attain $a^k=1-(1-x)^k$.
  Hence, maximality gives $F_k(\mathsf P)\ge a^k$, or $p\le p_0=(1-x)^k$.
  Suppose for a contradiction that $0<w<W_k$.
  We will apply \cref{lem:upper-intensity,lem:large-defect} and then compare the upper and lower bounds for $T_0$ to exclude this possibility.

  By {\cref{lem:crossing-lower-finite,lem:crossing-upper}}, we have $11/24<c_k<1/2$.
  Recall that $\delta=1-a$.
  Let $M$ and $D$ be as in \cref{sec:contact}, so
  \[
    M=\frac{x(1-F_{k-1}(\mathsf P))}{F_k(\mathsf P)-F_{k-1}(\mathsf P)}
    \text{ and }
    D=M-x.
  \]
  By {\cref{obs:contact-identities}\textup{\ref{item:contact-failure}} and \cref{cor:contact-moments}\textup{\ref{item:contact-moment-identity}}}, we have $x<M\le1$, $\mathsf P([0,M])=1$, and
  \[
    \operatorname{Var}(S_k)=D(r-\delta),\text{ and }
    \mathbb{P}(S_{k-1}<1-y)=\frac{p(M-y)}D
    \quad\text{for $\mathsf P$-almost every $y$.}
  \]
  By {\cref{lem:contact-moment}\textup{\ref{item:contact-moment-bounds}}}, we have $r\le M$.
  By {\cref{prop:finite-shortfall-margin}\textup{\ref{item:shortfall-ratio}}}, we have $D>3x$ and
  \[
    0\le\frac{M-r}{D}<\frac1{20}-\frac{3x}{20D}.
  \]

  By \cref{prop:support-separation}, we have $\mathsf P([x+D/16,x+17D/20])=0$ and $\mathsf P((x+17D/20,M])>0$.
  We use $q,X^{\operatorname{L}},X^{\operatorname{U}},x_0,\lambda$ from the conditional decomposition in \cref{sec:conditional-laws} with $\varepsilon=1/16$ and $\zeta=17/20$.
  The upper interval $(x+17D/20,M]$ has positive probability, so $q<1$, while $q\ge\mathsf P(\{0\})\ge1-a>0$.
  Recall that $A=M-x_0$, $J=X^{\operatorname{U}}-x_0$, $m=k(x-x_0)$, and $\eta=a-m/A$.
  Apply \cref{lem:upper-intensity} with $\varepsilon=1/16$ and $\zeta=17/20$.
  If $x_0=0$, then $\mathsf P=\mathsf B_x$ by \cref{lem:upper-intensity}\textup{\ref{item:upper-intensity-zero}}.
  Since $a=kx$, the decomposition $\mathsf P=(1-a)\delta_0+a\mathsf Q$ then implies $\mathsf Q=(1-1/k)\delta_0+(1/k)\delta_1$.
  Recall that $R_k=Y_1+\cdots+Y_k$.
  Since $\mathbb{E} R_k=1$ and $R_k$ takes nonnegative integer values,
  \[
    w=k\mathbb{E}(R_k-1)_+
    =k\mathbb{E}(1-R_k)_+
    =k\mathbb{P}(R_k=0)
    =k(1-1/k)^k
    =W_k,
  \]
  contrary to $0<w<W_k$.
  Thus, $x_0>0$, and \cref{lem:upper-intensity}\textup{\ref{item:upper-intensity-parameters}} gives $\lambda<a$, $J>m+\delta-x_0/5$ almost surely, and $0<\eta<a$.

  By the almost-everywhere equality in {\cref{obs:contact-identities}\textup{\ref{item:contact-equality}}} and the definition of $D$, we have $h(y)-h(0)=py/D$ for $\mathsf P$-almost every $y$.
  For independent $X,X'\sim\mathsf P$, {\cref{lem:contact-moment}\textup{\ref{item:contact-moment-formula}}} gives
  \[
    v=(r-\delta)(M-r)
    -\frac{k}{2p}\mathbb{E}\left[
      (X-X')\int_{X'}^X\bigl(h(t)-h(0)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d} t
      \right],
  \]
  where $v=\operatorname{Var}(S_k\mid S_k<1)$.

  Applying \cref{lem:large-defect} to $\mathsf P$, we obtain $\eta/a<1/10$.
  Since $0<\eta<a<1$, it follows that $0<\eta<1/10$.

  \begin{claim}\label{lem:small-defect-exclusion}
    We have $T_0<\eta/3$.
  \end{claim}
  \begin{proof}
    Applying \cref{lem:conditional-variance-bounds}\textup{\ref{item:conditional-variance-small}} and \cref{lem:conditional-support} with $\varepsilon=1/16$ and $\zeta=17/20$, we obtain
    \[
      b_0:=ess sup X^{\operatorname{L}}<\frac A{10},\text{ and }
      \mathcal V<\min\left\{5\eta,\frac1{25}\right\}.
    \]
    For independent copies $X_1^{\operatorname{L}},\ldots,X_k^{\operatorname{L}}$, the variables $(X_i^{\operatorname{L}}-x_0)/A$ are independent and centered.
    Since $0\le X_i^{\operatorname{L}},x_0\le b_0$, their absolute values are at most $b_0/A<1/10$, and their total variance is $\mathcal V$.
    Applying \cref{lem:exact-upper-count}\textup{\ref{item:exact-upper-count-tail}} and \cref{lem:small-conditional-tail}, we obtain
    \[
      T_0
      \le\mathbb{P}\left(\frac{B_k}{A}\ge1-\eta\right)
      <\frac{\eta}{3}.
    \]
  \end{proof}
  However, \cref{lem:exact-upper-count}\textup{\ref{item:exact-upper-count-tail}} gives $T_0>\eta/3$, a contradiction.

  By \cref{lem:critical}, every maximizing distribution has $0\le w\le W_k$.
  Since $0<w<W_k$ has been excluded, we have $w=0$ or $w=W_k$.
head: environment

label: lem:small-defect-exclusion
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{lem:small-defect-exclusion}
    We have $T_0<\eta/3$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Applying \cref{lem:conditional-variance-bounds}\textup{\ref{item:conditional-variance-small}} and \cref{lem:conditional-support} with $\varepsilon=1/16$ and $\zeta=17/20$, we obtain
    \[
      b_0:=ess sup X^{\operatorname{L}}<\frac A{10},\text{ and }
      \mathcal V<\min\left\{5\eta,\frac1{25}\right\}.
    \]
    For independent copies $X_1^{\operatorname{L}},\ldots,X_k^{\operatorname{L}}$, the variables $(X_i^{\operatorname{L}}-x_0)/A$ are independent and centered.
    Since $0\le X_i^{\operatorname{L}},x_0\le b_0$, their absolute values are at most $b_0/A<1/10$, and their total variance is $\mathcal V$.
    Applying \cref{lem:exact-upper-count}\textup{\ref{item:exact-upper-count-tail}} and \cref{lem:small-conditional-tail}, we obtain
    \[
      T_0
      \le\mathbb{P}\left(\frac{B_k}{A}\ge1-\eta\right)
      <\frac{\eta}{3}.
    \]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $k=1$, \cref{lem:dimension-one} gives $\Phi_1(x)=\min\{x,1\}$.
    Fix $k\ge2$ and set $a=k\beta_k$.
    By \cref{lem:attainment}, choose a law $\mathsf P$ maximizing $F_k$ among nonnegative Borel laws of mean at most $\beta_k$.
    By \cref{prop:normalization}, write $\mathsf P=(1-a)\delta_0+a\mathsf Q$, where $\mathsf Q\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])$ has mean $1/k$.
    By \cref{prop:maximizing-endpoints}, we have $w=0$ or $w=W_k$.
    Since $(1-a)/a=c_k/k\le1/(2k)<2/(k-1)$, \cref{prop:strict-chord} applies.
    At both endpoints, \cref{lem:initial-nodes}\textup{(ii)} gives $A(w)=H(w)$, and hence
    \[
      a^{-k}\Phi_k(\beta_k)
      =a^{-k}F_k(\mathsf P)
      \le1-H(w)+A(w)=1.
    \]
    Therefore $\Phi_k(\beta_k)\le(k\beta_k)^k$.
    Both $\mathsf B_{\beta_k}$ and $\mathsf C_{k,\beta_k}$ attain $(k\beta_k)^k=1-(1-\beta_k)^k$, so equality holds.
    The hypothesis of \cref{prop:mean-transfer} is now verified.
    It follows that $\Phi_k(x)=1-(1-x)^k$ for $0\le x<\beta_k$, that $\Phi_k(x)=(kx)^k$ for $\beta_k<x\le1/k$, and that $\Phi_k(x)=1$ for $x\ge1/k$.
    Together with the value at $\beta_k$, this proves the formula in \cref{thm:iid-tail} for every $k\ge1$ and $x\ge0$.
head: environment

label: lem:endpoint-laws
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:endpoint-laws}
  Let $k\ge2$ and let $\mathsf Q\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])$ have mean $1/k$.
  For independent $Y_1,\ldots,Y_k$ with law $\mathsf Q$, write $R_k=Y_1+\cdots+Y_k$ and $w=k\mathbb{E}(R_k-1)_+$.
  Then $w=0$ implies $\mathsf Q=\delta_{1/k}$, while $w=W_k$ implies $\mathsf Q=(1-1/k)\delta_0+(1/k)\delta_1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $w=0$, then $\mathbb{E}(R_k-1)_+=0$, so $R_k\le1$ almost surely.
  Since $\mathbb{E} R_k=1$, we conclude that $R_k=1$ almost surely.
  By independence, we have $k\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)=0$, and hence $\mathsf Q=\delta_{1/k}$.

  If $w=W_k$, then by independence and $\mathbb{E} Y_i=1/k$ we have
  \[
    \mathbb{E}(1-R_k)_+=\frac{w}{k}=\left(1-\frac1k\right)^k=\mathbb{E}\prod_{i=1}^k(1-Y_i).
  \]
  By \cref{lem:product-shortfall}\textup{(i)} with $y_i=Y_i$, we have $(1-R_k)_+\le\prod_{i=1}^k(1-Y_i)$ almost surely.
  Since the two sides have equal expectations, we obtain $(1-R_k)_+=\prod_{i=1}^k(1-Y_i)$ almost surely.
  If $\mathsf Q((0,1))>0$, then all $Y_1,\ldots,Y_k$ lie in $(0,1)$ with probability $\mathsf Q((0,1))^k>0$ by independence.
  On this event, \cref{lem:product-shortfall}\textup{(i)} implies $(1-R_k)_+<\prod_{i=1}^k(1-Y_i)$, contradicting the almost-sure equality $(1-R_k)_+=\prod_{i=1}^k(1-Y_i)$.
  Thus, $Y_1\in\{0,1\}$ almost surely, and $\mathbb{P}(Y_1=1)=\mathbb{E} Y_1=1/k$.
  Therefore, $\mathsf Q=(1-1/k)\delta_0+(1/k)\delta_1$.
head: environment

label: prop:crossing-equality
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:crossing-equality}
  Let $k\ge2$.
  Then $\Phi_k(\beta_k)=1-(1-\beta_k)^k=(k\beta_k)^k$.
  The maximizing nonnegative Borel laws under $m(\mathsf P)\le\beta_k$ are exactly $\mathsf B_{\beta_k}$ and $\mathsf C_{k,\beta_k}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cref{lem:attainment}, $F_k$ attains its maximum among nonnegative Borel laws with mean at most $\beta_k$.
  Fix an arbitrary maximizing law $\mathsf P$ under $m(\mathsf P)\le\beta_k$.
  By \cref{prop:normalization}\textup{(i)}, $\mathsf P$ is supported on $[0,1]$ and has mean $\beta_k$.
  By \cref{prop:normalization}, we can write $\mathsf P=(1-a)\delta_0+a\mathsf Q$ with $a=k\beta_k$ and $m(\mathsf Q)=1/k$.
  Let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_k$ be independent with law $\mathsf Q$ and set $w=k\mathbb{E}(Y_1+\cdots+Y_k-1)_+$.
  By \cref{prop:maximizing-endpoints}, $w=0$ or $w=W_k$.
    The numerical formula proved in \cref{sec:other-probability-consequences} gives $\Phi_k(\beta_k)=(k\beta_k)^k$.
    Both $\mathsf B_{\beta_k}$ and $\mathsf C_{k,\beta_k}$ have mean $\beta_k$, and
    \[
      F_k(\mathsf B_{\beta_k})
      =1-(1-\beta_k)^k
      =(k\beta_k)^k
      =F_k(\mathsf C_{k,\beta_k}).
    \]
    Thus both distributions are maximizing.

    By \cref{lem:endpoint-laws}, $w=0$ implies $\mathsf Q=\delta_{1/k}$, while $w=W_k$ implies $\mathsf Q=(1-1/k)\delta_0+(1/k)\delta_1$.
    Substituting into $\mathsf P=(1-a)\delta_0+a\mathsf Q$, we obtain $\mathsf P=\mathsf C_{k,\beta_k}$ when $w=0$ and $\mathsf P=\mathsf B_{\beta_k}$ when $w=W_k$.
    Since $\mathsf P$ was an arbitrary maximizing law, no other nonnegative Borel law with mean at most $\beta_k$ attains $\Phi_k(\beta_k)$.
    Conversely, the two displayed success probabilities show that both $\mathsf B_{\beta_k}$ and $\mathsf C_{k,\beta_k}$ attain this maximum.
    This proves the formula and all equality cases in \cref{prop:crossing-equality}.
head: environment

label: prop:equality-transfer
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:equality-transfer}
  Fix $k\ge2$.
  Suppose that the maximizing laws under $m(\mathsf P)\le\beta_k$ are exactly $\mathsf B_{\beta_k}$ and $\mathsf C_{k,\beta_k}$.
  Then the maximizing laws for every mean bound $x\ge0$ are characterized as follows.

  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]

    \item If $x=0$, then the unique maximizing law is $\delta_0$.

    \item If $0<x<{\beta_k}$, then the unique maximizing law is $\mathsf B_x$.

    \item If $x={\beta_k}$, then the maximizing laws are exactly $\mathsf B_{{\beta_k}}$ and $\mathsf C_{k,{\beta_k}}$.

    \item If $\beta_k<x<1/k$, then the unique maximizing law is $\mathsf C_{k,x}$.

    \item If $x=1/k$, then the unique maximizing law is $\delta_{1/k}$.

    \item If $x>1/k$, then a feasible law is maximizing if and only if it is supported on $[1/k,\infty)$.
  \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix an arbitrary $x\in(0,\beta_k)$ and an arbitrary maximizing law $\mathsf P$ under $m(\mathsf P)\le x$.
  Take $\theta=({\beta_k}-x)/(1-x)$.
  Then $m(\mathsf P_\theta^+)\le{\beta_k}$ and $1-F_k(\mathsf P_\theta^+)=(1-\theta)^k[1-F_k(\mathsf P)]$.
  Since $1-F_k(\mathsf P)=(1-x)^k$ and $1-\theta=(1-{\beta_k})/(1-x)$, we obtain $1-F_k(\mathsf P_\theta^+)=(1-{\beta_k})^k$.
  Thus, $\mathsf P_\theta^+$ maximizes $F_k$ under the mean bound $\beta_k$ and has positive mass at one.
  Since $\mathsf C_{k,{\beta_k}}$ has no mass at one, while $\mathsf P_\theta^+(\{1\})>0$, we must have $\mathsf P_\theta^+=\mathsf B_{{\beta_k}}$, which implies $\mathsf P=\mathsf B_x$.

  Now fix an arbitrary $x\in(\beta_k,1/k)$ and an arbitrary maximizing law $\mathsf P$ under $m(\mathsf P)\le x$.
  Take $q={\beta_k}/x\in(0,1)$, so $m(\mathsf P_q^-)\le{\beta_k}$.
  Since $m(\mathsf P_q^-)\le\beta_k$, the hypothesis gives $F_k(\mathsf P_q^-)\le(k\beta_k)^k$.
  Thus, \cref{fact:mixtures}\textup{(ii)} gives
  \[
    (k\beta_k)^k=q^kF_k(\mathsf P)\le F_k(\mathsf P_q^-)\le(k\beta_k)^k.
  \]
  Thus, equality holds, and \cref{fact:mixtures}\textup{(ii)} gives $F_j(\mathsf P)=0$ for every $1\le j<k$.
  In particular, $F_1(\mathsf P)=0$, so $\mathsf P(\{1\})=\mathsf P_q^-(\{1\})=0$.
  Since $m(\mathsf P_q^-)\le\beta_k$ and $F_k(\mathsf P_q^-)=(k\beta_k)^k=1-(1-\beta_k)^k$, the hypothesis of \cref{prop:equality-transfer} implies that $\mathsf P_q^-$ is either $\mathsf B_{\beta_k}$ or $\mathsf C_{k,\beta_k}$.
  Since $\mathsf P_q^-(\{1\})=0$ and $\mathsf B_{\beta_k}(\{1\})=\beta_k>0$, we have $\mathsf P_q^-=\mathsf C_{k,\beta_k}$, and hence $\mathsf P=\mathsf C_{k,x}$.

  Thus, among Borel probability laws $\mathsf P$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $m(\mathsf P)\le x$, the only possible maximizer is $\mathsf B_x$ when $0<x<\beta_k$ and $\mathsf C_{k,x}$ when $\beta_k<x<1/k$.
  Conversely,
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      F_k(\mathsf B_x)
       & =1-(1-x)^k=\Phi_k(x)
       &                      & (0<x<\beta_k),   \\
      F_k(\mathsf C_{k,x})
       & =(kx)^k=\Phi_k(x)
       &                      & (\beta_k<x<1/k).
    \end{aligned}
  \]

  At $x=\beta_k$, the hypothesis states that, among Borel probability laws $\mathsf P$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $m(\mathsf P)\le\beta_k$, the equality $F_k(\mathsf P)=1-(1-\beta_k)^k=(k\beta_k)^k$ holds if and only if $\mathsf P=\mathsf B_{\beta_k}$ or $\mathsf P=\mathsf C_{k,\beta_k}$.
  At $x=0$, nonnegativity forces $\mathsf P=\delta_0$.
  For $x\ge1/k$, the feasible law $\delta_{1/k}$ attains one.
  An i.i.d.\ law has success probability one exactly when it is supported on $[1/k,\infty)$.
  Indeed, if it assigns positive mass to $[0,1/k)$, then all $k$ observations lie there with positive probability and their sum is less than one.
  At mean bound $1/k$, support on $[1/k,\infty)$ forces $\delta_{1/k}$.
  For larger bounds it characterizes precisely the stated maximizing laws.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cref{lem:dimension-one}, $\Phi_1(x)=\min\{x,1\}$ for every $x\ge0$.
    For $0\le x\le1$, the unique maximizing law is $\mathsf B_x$.
    For $x>1$, a law with mean at most $x$ is maximizing if and only if it is supported on $[1,\infty)$.
    Thus, the formula and all equality statements hold for $k=1$.

    Fix $k\ge2$.
    By \cref{prop:crossing-equality}, every nonnegative Borel law $\mathsf P$ with $m(\mathsf P)\le\beta_k$ satisfies $F_k(\mathsf P)\le1-(1-\beta_k)^k=(k\beta_k)^k$, with equality exactly for $\mathsf B_{\beta_k}$ and $\mathsf C_{k,\beta_k}$.
    By \cref{prop:mean-transfer}, this bound at $\beta_k$ implies $F_k(\mathsf P)\le1-(1-x)^k$ for $0<x<\beta_k$ and $F_k(\mathsf P)\le(kx)^k$ for $\beta_k<x<1/k$, whenever $\mathsf P$ is a nonnegative Borel law with $m(\mathsf P)\le x$.
    These bounds are attained by $\mathsf B_x$ and $\mathsf C_{k,x}$, respectively.
    At $x=0$, nonnegativity forces $\mathsf P=\delta_0$, while for $x\ge1/k$, the feasible law $\delta_{1/k}$ attains probability one.
    Together with the value at $\beta_k$ and the comparison of the two candidate probabilities in \cref{prop:mean-transfer}, this proves
    \[
      \Phi_k(x)=
      \begin{cases}
        \max\{1-(1-x)^k,(kx)^k\}, & 0\le x\le1/k, \\
        1,                        & x\ge1/k.
      \end{cases}
    \]

    It remains to verify the equality statements for $k\ge2$.
    The classification at $\beta_k$ in \cref{prop:crossing-equality} verifies the hypothesis of \cref{prop:equality-transfer}.
    By \cref{prop:equality-transfer}\textup{(i)(ii)}, the unique maximizing law is $\mathsf B_x$ for $0\le x<\beta_k$, where $\mathsf B_0=\delta_0$.
    At $x=\beta_k$, \cref{prop:crossing-equality} identifies exactly the two maximizing laws $\mathsf B_{\beta_k}$ and $\mathsf C_{k,\beta_k}$.
    By \cref{prop:equality-transfer}\textup{(iv)(v)}, the unique maximizing law is $\mathsf C_{k,x}$ for $\beta_k<x\le1/k$, including $\mathsf C_{k,1/k}=\delta_{1/k}$ at $x=1/k$.
    These are precisely \textup{(ii)--(iv)} of \cref{thm:iid-tail}.
    Finally, by \cref{prop:equality-transfer}\textup{(vi)}, for $x>1/k$ a law with mean at most $x$ is maximizing if and only if it assigns probability one to $[1/k,\infty)$, proving \textup{(v)} for $k\ge2$.
    Together with the case $k=1$, this completes the proof of the formula and all equality cases in \cref{thm:iid-tail}.
