label: fact:construction-densities
title: Fact
head: environment

label: lem:approx-cover
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:approx-cover}
  Fix $k\ge2$, $0\le\xi<1/k$ and $\rho>0$.
  There exists an integer $n_0=n_0(k,\xi,\rho)$ such that, for every integer $n\ge n_0$, the following holds.
  If $0\le x\le\xi$ and $\mathcal H\subseteq\binom{[n]}k$ satisfies $\nu(\mathcal H)\le xn$, then there is a function $w:[n]\to[0,1]$ such that
  \[
    \sum_{v=1}^n w(v)\le(x+\rho)n,
  \]
  and all but at most $\rho n^k$ edges $E\in\mathcal H$ satisfy
  \[
    \sum_{v\in E}w(v)\ge1.
  \]
head: environment
name: Cao--Liu--Zhang

label: lem:matching-sequence
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first handle the case $R=k$.
  Choose any $(ks_i+k-1)$-set $Q_i\subseteq[n_i]$.
  Since $n_i-|Q_i|=o(n_i)$,
  \[
    \binom{n_i}k-C_k(s_i)
    \le(n_i-|Q_i|)\binom{n_i-1}{k-1}=o(n_i^k).
  \]
  Since $|\mathcal F_i|\ge D_k(n_i,s_i)-o(n_i^k)$ and $D_k(n_i,s_i)\ge C_k(s_i)$, we have $\binom{n_i}k-|\mathcal F_i|=o(n_i^k)$.
  Consequently,
  \[
    \left|\mathcal F_i\triangle\binom{Q_i}k\right|
    \le\left(\binom{n_i}k-C_k(s_i)\right)
    +\left(\binom{n_i}k-|\mathcal F_i|\right)=o(n_i^k).
  \]
  This proves both assertions when $R=k$.
  Henceforth assume $R>k$, and write $x=1/R$ and $x_i=s_i/n_i$.

  By \cref{fact:construction-densities} and $x_i\to x$, we have $D_k(n_i,s_i)/\binom{n_i}k\to\Phi_k(x)$.
For a fixed $\xi$ with $x<\xi<1/k$ and each integer $\ell\ge1$,
  let $n_0(\ell)$ be an integer supplied by \cref{lem:approx-cover}
  with $\rho=1/\ell$.
  Since $x_i\to x<\xi$ and $n_i\to\infty$, we may choose positive integers $a_\ell$ recursively as follows.
  For each integer $\ell\ge1$, choose $a_\ell$ such that $0\le x_i\le\xi$ and $n_i\ge n_0(\ell)$ for every $i\ge a_\ell$, taking $a_\ell>a_{\ell-1}$ when $\ell\ge2$.
  For each $i\ge a_1$, let $\ell$ be the unique integer with $a_\ell\le i<a_{\ell+1}$, and set $\epsilon_i=1/\ell$.
  For each such $i$, since $\nu(\mathcal F_i)\le s_i=x_i n_i$, apply \cref{lem:approx-cover} and choose a weight function $w_i:[n_i]\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{v=1}^{n_i}w_i(v)\le(x_i+\epsilon_i)n_i$ and $|\mathcal U_i|\le\epsilon_i n_i^k$, where $\mathcal U_i=\{E\in\mathcal F_i:\sum_{v\in E}w_i(v)<1\}$ is the family of sets not covered by $w_i$.
  We henceforth consider only $i\ge a_1$, since omitting finitely many initial terms does not affect the $o(n_i^k)$ conclusions of \cref{lem:matching-sequence}.

  As $i\to\infty$, the integer $\ell$ determined by $a_\ell\le i<a_{\ell+1}$ tends to infinity, so $\epsilon_i=1/\ell\to0$.
  Set $\mathsf P_i=\mathsf P_{w_i}=n_i^{-1}\sum_{v=1}^{n_i}\delta_{w_i(v)}$.
  By \eqref{eq:cover-sampling}, $m(\mathsf P_i)\le x_i+\epsilon_i$ and
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:sequence-success-lower-bound}
    F_k(\mathsf P_i)\ge\frac{k!}{n_i^k}(|\mathcal F_i|-|\mathcal U_i|)
    \ge\Phi_k(x)-o(1).
  \end{equation}
  The last inequality follows from $|\mathcal F_i|\ge D_k(n_i,s_i)-o(n_i^k)$, \cref{fact:construction-densities}, $k!\binom{n_i}{k}/n_i^k=1+o(1)$, and $\epsilon_i\to0$, together with $x_i\to x$ and the continuity of $\Phi_k$.

  Suppose that \textup{(i)} fails.
  After passing to a subsequence and relabelling, we may assume that there exists $\delta>0$ such that
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:sequence-distance-lower-bounds}
    \min\{d_C(\mathcal F_i),d_B(\mathcal F_i)\}\ge\delta n_i^k
    \text{ for every }i.
  \end{equation}
  By the weak sequential compactness of $\mathcal{P}([0,1])$, we may pass to a further subsequence, again relabelling, such that $\mathsf P_i$ converges weakly to some $\mathsf P\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])$.
  All limits in the remainder of the proof of \textup{(i)} are taken along this subsequence.
  By weak convergence on $[0,1]$, $m(\mathsf P)=\lim_{i\to\infty}m(\mathsf P_i)\le\lim_{i\to\infty}(x_i+\epsilon_i)=x$.
  By \cref{fact:weak-convergence}\textup{(ii)}, the product laws $\mathsf P_i^{\otimes k}$ converge weakly to $\mathsf P^{\otimes k}$.
  Applying \cref{thm:portmanteau}\textup{(iii)} to the closed set $H_k=\{(t_1,\ldots,t_k)\in[0,1]^k:t_1+\cdots+t_k\ge1\}$, we obtain
  \[
    \Phi_k(x)\le\limsup_{i\to\infty}\mathsf P_i^{\otimes k}(H_k)
    \le\mathsf P^{\otimes k}(H_k)=F_k(\mathsf P)\le\Phi_k(x).
  \]
  Here the first inequality follows from \eqref{eq:sequence-success-lower-bound}, and the last follows from $m(\mathsf P)\le x$ and the definition of $\Phi_k(x)$.
  Thus, $\mathsf P$ is a maximizing distribution.
  \Cref{thm:iid-tail} implies $\mathsf P\in\{\mathsf B_x,\mathsf C_{k,x}\}$.
  If $\mathsf P=\mathsf B_x$, then we will choose an $s_i$-set $S_i\subseteq[n_i]$ and take $\mathcal H_i=\mathcal A(S_i)$.
  If $\mathsf P=\mathsf C_{k,x}$, then we will choose a $(ks_i+k-1)$-set $Q_i\subseteq[n_i]$ and take $\mathcal H_i=\binom{Q_i}k$.
  The sets will be chosen so that
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:sequence-outside-edges}
    |\mathcal F_i\setminus\mathcal H_i|=o(n_i^k).
  \end{equation}

  \medskip
  \noindent{\bf Case 1. $\mathsf P=\mathsf B_x$.}
  \medskip

  We construct $S_i\subseteq[n_i]$ with $|S_i|=s_i$ and
  $|\mathcal F_i\setminus\mathcal A(S_i)|=o(n_i^k)$.
  Fix $0<\alpha<1/(2k)$.
  We first select the vertices with $w_i(v)>1-\alpha$ and then add or remove
  $o(n_i)$ vertices to obtain $|S_i|=s_i$.
  Define
  \[
    S_i'=\{v:w_i(v)>1-\alpha\}
    \text{ and }
    I_i^B=\{v:\alpha<w_i(v)\le1-\alpha\}.
  \]
  We have $\mathsf B_x((1-\alpha,1])=x$ and $\mathsf B_x((\alpha,1-\alpha])=0$.
  The intervals $(1-\alpha,1]$ and $(\alpha,1-\alpha]$ have boundaries of $\mathsf B_x$-measure zero in $[0,1]$.
  Since $\mathsf P_i$ converges weakly to $\mathsf B_x$, \cref{thm:portmanteau}\textup{(v)} implies
  \[
    \frac{|S_i'|}{n_i}=\mathsf P_i((1-\alpha,1])\to x
    \text{ and }
    \frac{|I_i^B|}{n_i}=\mathsf P_i((\alpha,1-\alpha])\to0.
  \]
  In particular, $|S_i'|=s_i+o(n_i)$ and $|I_i^B|=o(n_i)$.
  If a $k$-set $E$ avoids both $S_i'$ and $I_i^B$, then all its vertex weights are at most $\alpha$, and hence $\sum_{v\in E}w_i(v)\le k\alpha<1$.
  Thus, every edge of $\mathcal F_i\setminus\mathcal A(S_i')$ either belongs to $\mathcal U_i$ or meets $I_i^B$, and
  \[
    |\mathcal F_i\setminus\mathcal A(S_i')|
    \le|\mathcal U_i|+|I_i^B|\binom{n_i-1}{k-1}=o(n_i^k).
  \]
  For each $i$, choose an $s_i$-set $S_i$ by adding or removing exactly $\bigl||S_i'|-s_i\bigr|$ vertices from $S_i'$.
  We have $|S_i\triangle S_i'|=\bigl||S_i'|-s_i\bigr|=o(n_i)$.
  Only $k$-sets containing a changed vertex can change their membership in the cover family, so
  \[
    |\mathcal A(S_i')\triangle\mathcal A(S_i)|
    \le|S_i'\triangle S_i|\binom{n_i-1}{k-1}=o(n_i^k).
  \]
  Therefore, $\mathcal H_i=\mathcal A(S_i)$ satisfies \eqref{eq:sequence-outside-edges} and has size $M_k(n_i,s_i)$.

  \medskip
  \noindent{\bf Case 2. $\mathsf P=\mathsf C_{k,x}$.}
  \medskip

  We construct $Q_i\subseteq[n_i]$ with $|Q_i|=ks_i+k-1$ and
  $|\mathcal F_i\setminus\binom{Q_i}k|=o(n_i^k)$.
  Fix $0<\alpha<1/(2k^2)$.
  We first select the vertices with $|w_i(v)-1/k|\le\alpha$ and then add or remove
  $o(n_i)$ vertices to obtain $|Q_i|=ks_i+k-1$.
  Define
  \[
    Q_i'=\{v:|w_i(v)-1/k|\le\alpha\}
    \text{ and }
    I_i^C=\{v:w_i(v)>\alpha\}\setminus Q_i'.
  \]
  Since $1/k-\alpha>\alpha$, we have $Q_i'\subseteq\{v:w_i(v)>\alpha\}$.
  The intervals $[1/k-\alpha,1/k+\alpha]$ and $(\alpha,1]$ have boundaries of $\mathsf C_{k,x}$-measure zero in $[0,1]$.
  Both intervals contain $1/k$ and exclude $0$, so their $\mathsf C_{k,x}$-measure is $kx$.
  Since $\mathsf P_i$ converges weakly to $\mathsf C_{k,x}$, \cref{thm:portmanteau}\textup{(v)} implies
  \[
    \frac{|Q_i'|}{n_i}
    =\mathsf P_i([1/k-\alpha,1/k+\alpha])\to kx
    \text{ and }
    \frac{|I_i^C|}{n_i}
    =\mathsf P_i((\alpha,1])-\frac{|Q_i'|}{n_i}\to0.
  \]
  In particular, $|Q_i'|=ks_i+o(n_i)$ and $|I_i^C|=o(n_i)$.
  If a $k$-set $E$ is not contained in $Q_i'$ and avoids $I_i^C$, then at least one of its vertices has weight at most $\alpha$, and all the others have weight at most $1/k+\alpha$.
  Thus,
  \[
    \sum_{v\in E}w_i(v)\le\alpha+(k-1)(1/k+\alpha)
    =\frac{k-1}{k}+k\alpha<1.
  \]
  Every edge of $\mathcal F_i\setminus\binom{Q_i'}k$ therefore either belongs to $\mathcal U_i$ or meets $I_i^C$, so
  \[
    \left|\mathcal F_i\setminus\binom{Q_i'}k\right|
    \le|\mathcal U_i|+|I_i^C|\binom{n_i-1}{k-1}=o(n_i^k).
  \]
  Since $ks_i+k-1\le n_i$, for each $i$ choose a $(ks_i+k-1)$-set $Q_i$ by adding or removing exactly $\bigl||Q_i'|-(ks_i+k-1)\bigr|$ vertices from $Q_i'$.
  Since $k$ is fixed, we have $|Q_i\triangle Q_i'|=\bigl||Q_i'|-(ks_i+k-1)\bigr|=o(n_i)$.
  As only $k$-sets containing a changed vertex can change their membership in the clique family,
  \[
    \left|\binom{Q_i'}k\triangle\binom{Q_i}k\right|
    \le|Q_i'\triangle Q_i|\binom{n_i-1}{k-1}=o(n_i^k).
  \]
  Therefore, $\mathcal H_i=\binom{Q_i}k$ satisfies \eqref{eq:sequence-outside-edges} and has size $C_k(s_i)$.

  \medskip
  In either case, $|\mathcal H_i|\le D_k(n_i,s_i)$.
  Since $|\mathcal F_i|\ge D_k(n_i,s_i)-o(n_i^k)$, the bound $|\mathcal H_i|\le D_k(n_i,s_i)$ and \eqref{eq:sequence-outside-edges} give
  \[
    |\mathcal F_i\triangle\mathcal H_i|
    =2|\mathcal F_i\setminus\mathcal H_i|+|\mathcal H_i|-|\mathcal F_i|\le2|\mathcal F_i\setminus\mathcal H_i|+o(n_i^k)
    =o(n_i^k).
  \]
  This contradicts \eqref{eq:sequence-distance-lower-bounds}, proving \textup{(i)} along the whole original sequence.

  To prove \textup{(ii)}, we return to the original sequence and compare the sizes of the cover and clique families.
  Taking the minima in the definitions of $d_B(\mathcal F_i)$ and $d_C(\mathcal F_i)$, and using $|\mathcal F_i|\ge D_k(n_i,s_i)-o(n_i^k)$, we obtain
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      d_B(\mathcal F_i) & \ge|\mathcal F_i|-M_k(n_i,s_i)\ge D_k(n_i,s_i)-M_k(n_i,s_i)-o(n_i^k), \\
      d_C(\mathcal F_i) & \ge|\mathcal F_i|-C_k(s_i)\ge D_k(n_i,s_i)-C_k(s_i)-o(n_i^k).
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  If $k<R<\rho_k$, then $x=1/R>\beta_k$, and \cref{fact:construction-densities} implies
  \[
    \frac{C_k(s_i)-M_k(n_i,s_i)}{n_i^k}
    \longrightarrow\frac{(kx)^k-1+(1-x)^k}{k!}>0.
  \]
  Thus, $d_B(\mathcal F_i)\ge c n_i^k$ for some $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $i$.
  By \textup{(i)}, we have $d_C(\mathcal F_i)=o(n_i^k)$.
  If $R>\rho_k$, then $x=1/R<\beta_k$, and \cref{fact:construction-densities} implies
  \[
    \frac{M_k(n_i,s_i)-C_k(s_i)}{n_i^k}
    \longrightarrow\frac{1-(1-x)^k-(kx)^k}{k!}>0.
  \]
  Thus, $d_C(\mathcal F_i)\ge c n_i^k$ for some $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $i$.
  By \textup{(i)}, we have $d_B(\mathcal F_i)=o(n_i^k)$.
  Together with the case $R=k$ proved above, this establishes \textup{(ii)}.
head: environment

label: thm:bde
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:bde}
  Let $k\ge3$, $b\ge1$, and $n>2k^3b$ be integers.
  If $\mathcal J\subseteq\binom{[n]}k$ satisfies $\nu(\mathcal J)\le b$ and no $b$-set meets every edge of $\mathcal J$, then
  \[
    |\mathcal J|\le M_k(n,b)-\binom{n-b-k}{k-1}+1.
  \]
head: environment
name: Bollob\'as, Daykin and Erd\H{o}s

label: lem:sparse-emc
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sparse-emc}
  Let $k\ge3$, $n\ge k$, and $b\ge0$ be integers with $b\le n/(4k^3)$.
  If $\mathcal J\subseteq\binom{[n]}k$ satisfies $\nu(\mathcal J)\le b$, then $|\mathcal J|\le M_k(n,b)$.
  Equality holds if and only if $\mathcal J=\mathcal A(B')$ for some $b$-set $B'\subseteq[n]$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The case $b=0$ is immediate.
  Suppose $b\ge1$.
  If no $b$-set meets every edge of $\mathcal J$, then $n\ge4k^3b>2k^3b$, and by \cref{thm:bde}, we have
  \[
    |\mathcal J|\le M_k(n,b)-\binom{n-b-k}{k-1}+1<M_k(n,b).
  \]
  The strict inequality follows from $\binom{n-b-k}{k-1}>1$.
  Otherwise, $\mathcal J\subseteq\mathcal A(B')$ for some $b$-set $B'$, and equality holds exactly when $\mathcal J=\mathcal A(B')$.
head: environment

label: lem:local-cover
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:local-cover}
  Fix an integer $k\ge3$ and real constants $k<R<L$.
  There exist $\delta=\delta(k,R,L)>0$ and an integer $s_0=s_0(k,R,L)$ such that the following holds whenever $s,n$ are integers with $s\ge s_0$ and $Rs\le n\le Ls$.
  If $\mathcal F\subseteq\binom{[n]}k$ satisfies $\nu(\mathcal F)\le s$ and $|\mathcal A(S)\setminus\mathcal F|\le\delta n^k$ for some $s$-set $S\subseteq[n]$, then
  \[
    |\mathcal F|\le M_k(n,s),
  \]
  with equality exactly when $\mathcal F=\mathcal A(S')$ for some $s$-set $S'\subseteq[n]$.
  Moreover, for every $s$-set $S\subseteq[n]$ satisfying $|\mathcal A(S)\setminus\mathcal F|\le\delta n^k$, there is a set $B\subseteq S$ such that
  \[
    \nu(\mathcal F[U])\le |B|\le\frac{|U|}{4k^3},
  \]
  where $U=([n]\setminus S)\cup B$.
head: environment

label: eq:cover-b-small
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\gamma=R-k>0$.
  Choose $\delta=\delta(k,R,L)>0$ sufficiently small, and then choose $s_0=s_0(k,R,L)$ sufficiently large for the estimates below.
  Fix any $s$-set $S\subseteq[n]$ with $|\mathcal A(S)\setminus\mathcal F|\le\delta n^k$, and set $W=[n]\setminus S$.
  For each $v\in S$, let $m(v)$ be the number of missing edges whose unique vertex in $S$ is $v$.
  Thus,
  \[
    m(v)=\left|\left\{A\in\binom W{k-1}:
    A\cup\{v\}\notin\mathcal F\right\}\right|.
  \]
  Set $D_0=\binom{\lfloor\gamma s/2\rfloor}{k-1}$ and $B=\{v\in S:m(v)\ge D_0\}$.
  Write $b=|B|$.
  Since no missing edge is counted for two vertices of $S$, we have $bD_0\le|\mathcal A(S)\setminus\mathcal F|\le\delta n^k$.
  Set $U=W\cup B$ and $N=|U|=n-s+b$.
  Since $D_0=\Theta_{k,R}(s^{k-1})$ and $n\le Ls$, we have $b\le\delta L^k s^k/D_0=O_{k,R,L}(\delta s)$.
  Since $N\ge(R-1)s$ and $\delta$ is sufficiently small, we may assume that
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:cover-b-small}
    b\le s/3,\text{ } b\le\gamma s/4\text{ and }b\le N/(4k^3).
  \end{equation}
  We also have $\gamma s\ge4$ and $N\ge k$ by the choice of $s_0$.

  We claim that the family $\mathcal F[U]$ has matching number at most $b$.
  Suppose for a contradiction that $\mathcal F[U]$ contains a matching $\mathcal M_0$ of $b+1$ edges.
  Write $S\setminus B=\{v_1,\ldots,v_{s-b}\}$.
  Since $U=W\cup B$, the edges of $\mathcal M_0$ avoid $S\setminus B$.
  Fix any integer $j$ with $0\le j<s-b$ and any edges $E_t=\{v_t\}\cup A_t\in\mathcal F$, with $A_t\in\binom W{k-1}$ for $1\le t\le j$, such that $\mathcal M_0\cup\{E_1,\ldots,E_j\}$ is a matching.
  The edges of $\mathcal M_0$ use at most $k(b+1)$ vertices of $W$, and the $j$ added edges use $j(k-1)$ more.
  Since $j\le s-b-1$, $n\ge(k+\gamma)s$, $b\le\gamma s/4$ by \eqref{eq:cover-b-small}, and $\gamma s\ge4$, the number of unused vertices of $W$ is at least
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      |W|-k(b+1)-j(k-1)
       & \ge |W|-k(b+1)-(s-b-1)(k-1) \\
       & =n-ks-b-1
      \ge\gamma s-b-1
      \ge\lfloor\gamma s/2\rfloor.
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  Among the unused vertices there are at least $D_0$ choices of $A\in\binom W{k-1}$.
  Since $v_{j+1}\notin B$, we have $m(v_{j+1})<D_0$, so one such $A$ satisfies $\{v_{j+1}\}\cup A\in\mathcal F$.
  Choose one such set as $A_{j+1}$, and set $E_{j+1}=\{v_{j+1}\}\cup A_{j+1}$.
  The edge $E_{j+1}$ is disjoint from the current matching because $v_{j+1}$ is new and $A_{j+1}$ uses only unused vertices of $W$.
  After all $s-b$ vertices have been processed, the matching has $(b+1)+(s-b)=s+1$ edges, a contradiction.

  Every edge of $\mathcal F$ either meets $S\setminus B$ or belongs to $\mathcal F[U]$.
  We have $\nu(\mathcal F[U])\le b$ and $b\le N/(4k^3)$.
  By \cref{lem:sparse-emc}, we have
  \[
    |\mathcal F|\le\binom nk-\binom Nk+|\mathcal F[U]|
    \le\binom nk-\binom{N-b}k=M_k(n,s),
  \]
  where $N-b=n-s$.
  Equality forces $\mathcal F[U]=\mathcal A_U(B')$ for a $b$-set $B'\subseteq U$ and requires every $k$-set meeting $S\setminus B$ to belong to $\mathcal F$.
  Thus, $\mathcal F=\mathcal A((S\setminus B)\cup B')$, whose center has size $s$.
  Conversely, $|\mathcal A(S')|=M_k(n,s)$ for every $s$-set $S'$.

label: lem:large-clique-emc
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:large-clique-emc}
  For each fixed $k\ge3$, there exist $\eta>0$ and $s_0$ such that the following holds whenever $s\ge s_0$ and $k(s+1)\le n\le(k+1/2)s$.
  If $\mathcal H\subseteq\binom{[n]}k$ satisfies $\nu(\mathcal H)\le s$ and $\omega(\mathcal H)\ge(1-\eta)ks$, then $|\mathcal H|\le C_k(s)$.
  Equality holds if and only if $\mathcal H=\binom Uk$ for some $(ks+k-1)$-set $U\subseteq[n]$.
head: environment

label: lem:local-clique
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{lem:local-clique}
  For each fixed $k\ge3$, there exist $\delta>0$ and $s_0$ such that the following holds whenever $s\ge s_0$ and $k(s+1)\le n\le(k+1/2)s$.
  If $\mathcal F\subseteq\binom{[n]}k$ satisfies $\nu(\mathcal F)\le s$ and $|\binom Qk\setminus\mathcal F|\le\delta n^k$ for some $(ks+k-1)$-set $Q\subseteq[n]$, then $|\mathcal F|\le C_k(s)$.
  Equality holds if and only if $\mathcal F=\binom{Q'}k$ for some $(ks+k-1)$-set $Q'\subseteq[n]$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose $0<\eta<1$ as in \cref{lem:large-clique-emc}, and choose $s_0$ sufficiently large.
  Choose $0<\delta<(\eta/(2k+1))^k$.
  Let $s,n$ and $\mathcal F$ satisfy the hypotheses of \cref{lem:local-clique}.
  Fix a $(ks+k-1)$-set $Q\subseteq[n]$ such that $|\binom Qk\setminus\mathcal F|\le\delta n^k$.
  By relabelling, we may assume that $Q=[m]$, where $m=ks+k-1$.
  For distinct vertices $a,b\in[n]$ and a family $\mathcal G\subseteq\binom{[n]}k$, define the shift $S_{ab}(\mathcal G)$ by replacing each edge $E\in\mathcal G$ with $b\in E$, $a\notin E$ and $(E\setminus\{b\})\cup\{a\}\notin\mathcal G$ by $(E\setminus\{b\})\cup\{a\}$.
  All other edges remain unchanged.
  Let $\mathcal F'$ be obtained from $\mathcal F$ by repeatedly applying shifts $S_{ab}$ with $1\le a<b\le m$ until no such shift changes the family.
  Each shift preserves the size of the family and does not increase its matching number.
  Since both shifted vertices lie in $Q$, the number of missing edges in $Q$ also remains unchanged.

  Set $h=\lceil(1-\eta)ks\rceil$.
  We show that every $k$-set in $[h]$ belongs to $\mathcal F'$.
  Suppose for a contradiction that there exists $A\in\binom{[h]}k\setminus\mathcal F'$, and fix one such $A$.
  Fix an arbitrary $B\in\binom{\{h+1,\ldots,m\}}k$.
  If $B\in\mathcal F'$, then replacing its vertices one at a time by the vertices of $A$ would keep every resulting $k$-set in $\mathcal F'$, since every vertex of $A$ is smaller than every vertex of $B$ and $\mathcal F'$ is unchanged by all shifts $S_{ab}$ with $1\le a<b\le m$.
  This would give $A\in\mathcal F'$, contrary to the choice of $A$.
  Since $B$ was arbitrary, every $k$-set in $\{h+1,\ldots,m\}$ is missing from $\mathcal F'$.
  By our choice of $s_0$, we have $m-h\ge\eta ks+k-2\ge\max\{k,\eta ks/2\}$.
  Therefore,
  \[
    \left|\binom Qk\setminus\mathcal F'\right|
    \ge\binom{m-h}k
    \ge\left(\frac{m-h}{k}\right)^k
    \ge(\eta s/2)^k
    >\delta n^k,
  \]
  where the last inequality follows from $n\le(k+1/2)s$ and $\delta<(\eta/(2k+1))^k$.
  This contradicts $|\binom Qk\setminus\mathcal F'|=|\binom Qk\setminus\mathcal F|\le\delta n^k$.
  Hence, $[h]$ is a clique in $\mathcal F'$, so $\omega(\mathcal F')\ge(1-\eta)ks$.
  We also have $\nu(\mathcal F')\le s$.
  By \cref{lem:large-clique-emc}, we have $|\mathcal F|=|\mathcal F'|\le C_k(s)$.

  Suppose that $|\mathcal F|=C_k(s)$.
  The equality case of \cref{lem:large-clique-emc} implies $\mathcal F'=\binom{U_t}k$ for some $m$-set $U_t$.
  Write the sequence of shifts as $\mathcal F=\mathcal F^{(0)},\mathcal F^{(1)},\ldots,\mathcal F^{(t)}=\mathcal F'$, where $\mathcal F^{(\ell)}=S_{a_\ell b_\ell}(\mathcal F^{(\ell-1)})$ for $1\le\ell\le t$.
  Every $\mathcal F^{(\ell)}$ has $C_k(s)$ members and matching number at most $s$.
  We prove by reverse induction that every $\mathcal F^{(\ell)}$ is a clique family on $m$ vertices.
  The assertion holds for $\ell=t$.
  Suppose that $1\le\ell\le t$ and $\mathcal F^{(\ell)}=\binom{U_\ell}k$, where $|U_\ell|=m$.
  Since $S_{a_\ell b_\ell}$ only affects sets containing $a_\ell$ or $b_\ell$, every $k$-set in $U_\ell\setminus\{a_\ell,b_\ell\}$ also belongs to $\mathcal F^{(\ell-1)}$.
  Thus, $\mathcal F^{(\ell-1)}$ contains a clique on $U_\ell\setminus\{a_\ell,b_\ell\}$, whose size satisfies $|U_\ell\setminus\{a_\ell,b_\ell\}|\ge ks+k-3\ge ks\ge(1-\eta)ks$.
  The equality case of \cref{lem:large-clique-emc} therefore implies $\mathcal F^{(\ell-1)}=\binom{U_{\ell-1}}k$ for some $m$-set $U_{\ell-1}$.
  The induction shows that $\mathcal F=\binom{U_0}k$.
  Conversely, every clique family on $m$ vertices has $C_k(s)$ members.
head: environment

label: fact:large-clique-deficit
title: Fact
body_md:
\label{fact:large-clique-deficit}
  Let $k\ge3$ be an integer and $0<\eta\le1/(64k^4)$.
  Let $n,s$ be positive integers such that $s\ge60k^4$, $\eta ks\ge k-1$, and $k(s+1)\le n\le(k+1/2)s$.
  Let $\mathcal H'\subseteq\binom{[n]}k$ be $s$-saturated, with $u=\omega(\mathcal H')\ge(1-\eta)ks$, and set $d=ks+k-1-u$.
  Then
  \[
    C_k(s)-|\mathcal H'|
    \ge d\binom{ks}{k-1}
    \left[2-\left(\frac n{ks}\right)^{k-1}-5k^3\eta-\frac{3k^3}{s}\right].
  \]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $m=ks+k-1$, and let $Q$ be a largest clique in $\mathcal H'$, of order $u$.
  Then $(1-\eta)ks\le u\le m$.

  Set $d=m-u\ge0$.
  The range $k(s+1)\le n\le(k+1/2)s$ implies $s\ge2k$.
  Since $u<n$ and $Q$ is a largest clique, there is a missing $k$-set with exactly $k-1$ vertices in $Q$.
  Since $\mathcal H'$ is $s$-saturated, adding this set creates an $(s+1)$-edge matching containing it, and the remaining $s$ edges form a matching in $\mathcal H'$.
  Choose an $s$-edge matching $\mathcal M$ in $\mathcal H'$ maximizing $|Q\cup V(\mathcal M)|$, and let $\mathcal M'=\{E\in \mathcal M:E\not\subseteq Q\}$.
  Every $s$-edge matching leaves at most $k-1$ vertices of $Q$ uncovered, since otherwise one more clique edge could be added.
  In particular, $|Q\cup V(\mathcal M)|=ks+|Q\setminus V(\mathcal M)|\le m$.
  The matching obtained by deleting the added missing set leaves its $k-1$ vertices in $Q$ uncovered.
  By the choice of $\mathcal M$, we have $|Q\cup V(\mathcal M)|=ks+k-1=m$.
  Write $T=Q\cup V(\mathcal M)$, $B=V(\mathcal M')$, and $r=|\mathcal M'|$.
  Then $|T\setminus Q|=d$.

  Since $|T|=ks+k-1$, we have
  \[
    C_k(s)-|\mathcal H'|
    =\left|\binom Tk\setminus\mathcal H'\right|
    -\left|\mathcal H'\setminus\binom Tk\right|.
  \]
  We first bound $\left|\binom Tk\setminus\mathcal H'\right|$ from below and then $\left|\mathcal H'\setminus\binom Tk\right|$ from above.

  Each edge of $\mathcal M'$ contains a vertex outside $Q$, so $r\le d$.
  Since $\eta ks\ge k-1$ and $\eta\le1/(64k^4)$, we have $0\le d\le\eta ks+k-1\le2\eta ks\le s/2$.
  Also, $|Q\setminus B|=u-(kr-d)=k(s-r)+k-1$.
  If $E\in\mathcal H'$ satisfies $E\not\subseteq Q$ and $E\cap B=\emptyset$, then $|Q\setminus(B\cup E)|\ge|Q\setminus B|-(k-1)=k(s-r)$.
  Choose $k(s-r)$ vertices of $Q\setminus(B\cup E)$ and partition them into $s-r$ clique edges.
  Together with $\mathcal M'$ and $E$, these form a matching of size $s+1$.
  Thus, every edge not contained in $Q$ meets $B$.

  To count the missing $k$-sets in $T$, for each $v\in T\setminus Q$ define
  \[
    d_Q(v)=\left|\left\{D\in\binom Q{k-1}:D\cup\{v\}\in\mathcal H'\right\}\right|.
  \]

  We claim that $d_Q(v)\le(k-1)d\binom u{k-2}$ for every $v\in T\setminus Q$.
  Suppose for a contradiction that $d_Q(v)>(k-1)d\binom u{k-2}$ for some $v\in T\setminus Q$.
  By the maximality of $Q$, there is a missing set $e=\{v\}\cup D$ with $D\in\binom Q{k-1}$.
  Let $\mathcal N$ be an $(s+1)$-edge matching in $\mathcal H'\cup\{e\}$ containing $e$, and let $\mathcal N'=\{E\in \mathcal N\setminus\{e\}:E\not\subseteq Q\}$.
  Since $\mathcal N\setminus\{e\}$ is an $s$-edge matching in $\mathcal H'$, the choice of $\mathcal M$ implies $|V(\mathcal N')\setminus Q|\le d$.
  Consequently, $|\mathcal N'|\le d$ and $|V(\mathcal N')\cap Q|\le(k-1)d$.
  Choose $D'\in\binom{Q\setminus V(\mathcal N')}{k-1}$ such that $e'=\{v\}\cup D'\in\mathcal H'$.
  Indeed, for each vertex of $V(\mathcal N')\cap Q$, choosing the other $k-2$ vertices produces exactly $\binom{u-1}{k-2}$ members of $\binom Q{k-1}$ containing it.
  Since $v\in T\setminus Q$, we have $d\ge1$, so the number of members of $\binom Q{k-1}$ meeting $V(\mathcal N')$ is at most $|V(\mathcal N')\cap Q|\binom{u-1}{k-2}<(k-1)d\binom u{k-2}$.
  Since $d_Q(v)>(k-1)d\binom u{k-2}$, at least one of the sets counted by $d_Q(v)$ avoids $V(\mathcal N')$.
  Since $v\notin V(\mathcal N')$ and $D'$ avoids $V(\mathcal N')$, the family $\mathcal N'\cup\{e'\}$ is a matching.
  Note that $\mathcal N$ consists of $\mathcal N'$, the added set $e$, and $s-|\mathcal N'|$ edges contained in $Q$.
  Both $e$ and $e'$ use exactly $k-1$ vertices of $Q$, so
  \[
    |Q\setminus(V(\mathcal N')\cup e')|
    \ge k(s-|\mathcal N'|).
  \]
  Choose $k(s-|\mathcal N'|)$ of these unused vertices and partition them into $s-|\mathcal N'|$ clique edges.
  Together with $\mathcal N'$ and $e'$, these edges form a matching of size $s+1$ in $\mathcal H'$, a contradiction.
  This shows that $d_Q(v)\le(k-1)d\binom u{k-2}$ for every $v\in T\setminus Q$.

  The sets consisting of one vertex of $T\setminus Q$ and $k-1$ vertices of $Q$ are distinct for different outside vertices.
  Hence, summing the bound on $d_Q(v)$ over these $d$ vertices, we obtain
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:glp-missing-edges}
    \left|\binom Tk\setminus\mathcal H'\right|
    \ge d\binom u{k-1}-(k-1)d^2\binom u{k-2}.
  \end{equation}

  We now bound the edges outside $\binom Tk$.
  Let $W=[n]\setminus T$.
  Every edge of $\mathcal H'\setminus\binom Tk$ meets both $W$ and $B$, so we split these edges into
  \[
    \mathcal E_1=\left\{E\in\mathcal H'\setminus\binom Tk:|E\cap B|=1\right\}
    \text{ and }
    \mathcal E_2=\left\{E\in\mathcal H'\setminus\binom Tk:|E\cap B|\ge2\right\}.
  \]
  Since $r\le d$, we obtain
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:glp-multiple-intersections}
    |\mathcal E_2|\le\binom{kr}{2}\binom n{k-2}
    \le\frac{k^2d^2}{2}\binom n{k-2}.
  \end{equation}

  Each edge of $\mathcal E_1$ has a unique vertex $b\in B$, and its remaining $k-1$ vertices avoid $B$ and meet $W$.
  We therefore define
  \[
    \mathcal L=\left\{L\in\binom{[n]\setminus B}{k-1}:L\cap W\ne\emptyset\right\}.
  \]
  Every edge of $\mathcal E_1$ has a unique representation $\{b\}\cup L$ with $b\in B$ and $L\in\mathcal L$.
  For $b\in B$, let $a(b)=\left|\{L\in\mathcal L:\{b\}\cup L\in\mathcal H'\}\right|$.
  To bound $|\mathcal E_1|=\sum_{b\in B}a(b)$, we estimate $\sum_{b\in F}a(b)$ for each $F\in \mathcal M'$.
  Fix $F\in \mathcal M'$ and write $\ell_F=|F\setminus Q|$.
  We first prove the following claim.

  \begin{claim}\label{clm:large-clique-e1-matching}
    There is no matching of size $\ell_F+1$ in $\mathcal E_1$ such that every edge meets $F$.
  \end{claim}

  \begin{proof}
    Suppose for a contradiction that $E_1,\ldots,E_{\ell_F+1}$ form such a matching.
    Each $E_j$ meets $B$ only in a single vertex of $F$, so it is disjoint from all the edges in $\mathcal M'\setminus\{F\}$.
    Replacing $F$ by these edges produces a matching $\widetilde{\mathcal M}=(\mathcal M'\setminus\{F\})\cup\{E_1,\ldots,E_{\ell_F+1}\}$ in $\mathcal H'$, so $|\widetilde{\mathcal M}|\le s$.
    Deleting $F$ removes $\ell_F$ vertices outside $Q$, while the new edges add at least $\ell_F+1$ distinct vertices of $W$.
    This implies $|V(\widetilde{\mathcal M})\setminus Q|\ge d+1$.
    Thus, $|Q\cup V(\widetilde{\mathcal M})|\ge u+d+1=k(s+1)$.
    Hence, we have $|Q\setminus V(\widetilde{\mathcal M})|=|Q\cup V(\widetilde{\mathcal M})|-k|\widetilde{\mathcal M}|\ge k(s+1-|\widetilde{\mathcal M}|)$.
    Choose $k(s+1-|\widetilde{\mathcal M}|)$ of these unused vertices and partition them into $s+1-|\widetilde{\mathcal M}|$ clique edges.
    Together with $\widetilde{\mathcal M}$, they form an $(s+1)$-matching in $\mathcal H'$, a contradiction.
  \end{proof}

  Set $A=(k-1)^2\binom n{k-2}$.
  We next show that at most $\ell_F$ vertices $b\in F$ satisfy $a(b)>A$.
  Otherwise, choose distinct $b_1,\ldots,b_{\ell_F+1}\in F$ with $a(b_j)>A$.
  We can choose pairwise disjoint sets $L_j\in\mathcal L$ successively, with $\{b_j\}\cup L_j\in\mathcal H'$.
  Fix any integer $j$ with $1\le j\le\ell_F+1$ and any pairwise disjoint sets $L_1,\ldots,L_{j-1}\in\mathcal L$ satisfying $\{b_t\}\cup L_t\in\mathcal H'$ for every $1\le t<j$.
  Note that $j\le\ell_F+1\le k$, since the $b_j$'s are distinct vertices of the $k$-set $F$.
  At step $j$, the previously chosen $L_1,\ldots,L_{j-1}$ occupy at most $(j-1)(k-1)\le(k-1)^2$ vertices.
  For each such vertex $v$, at most $\binom{n-1}{k-2}\le\binom n{k-2}$ candidates counted by $a(b_j)$ contain $v$.
  Thus, at most $A$ sets counted by $a(b_j)$ meet $\bigcup_{t=1}^{j-1}L_t$, and $a(b_j)>A$ allows us to choose $L_j$ disjoint from $\bigcup_{t=1}^{j-1}L_t$.
  Every $L_j$ avoids $B$, so the $\ell_F+1$ edges $\{b_j\}\cup L_j$ form a matching in $\mathcal E_1$ in which every edge meets $F$, contradicting \cref{clm:large-clique-e1-matching}.
  Thus, $\sum_{b\in F}a(b)\le\ell_F|\mathcal L|+kA$ for every $F\in \mathcal M'$.

  Summing over $F\in \mathcal M'$, we obtain
  \[
    |\mathcal E_1|=\sum_{b\in B}a(b)
    =\sum_{F\in \mathcal M'}\sum_{b\in F}a(b)
    \le d|\mathcal L|+krA
    \le d|\mathcal L|+k(k-1)^2d\binom n{k-2}.
  \]
  Here $\sum_{F\in \mathcal M'}\ell_F=\sum_{F\in \mathcal M'}|F\setminus Q|=|T\setminus Q|=d$, since every vertex of $T\setminus Q$ lies in exactly one edge of $\mathcal M'$.
  The last inequality uses $r\le d$.
  Every $L\in\mathcal L$ meets $W\subseteq[n]\setminus Q$, so $|\mathcal L|\le\binom n{k-1}-\binom u{k-1}$.
  Therefore,
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:glp-single-intersections}
    |\mathcal E_1|
    \le d\left(\binom n{k-1}-\binom u{k-1}\right)
    +k(k-1)^2d\binom n{k-2}.
  \end{equation}

  Combining \eqref{eq:glp-missing-edges}, \eqref{eq:glp-multiple-intersections} and \eqref{eq:glp-single-intersections}, and using $\binom u{k-2}\le\binom n{k-2}$, we obtain
  \[
    C_k(s)-|\mathcal H'|
    \ge d\left[2\binom u{k-1}-\binom n{k-1}
      -\left(\left(k-1+\frac{k^2}{2}\right)d+k(k-1)^2\right)\binom n{k-2}\right].
  \]
  We compare the three binomial coefficients with $\binom{ks}{k-1}$.
  For $s\ge2k$, we have $ks-j\ge ks/2$ for $0\le j\le k-2$.
  Since $u\ge(1-\eta)ks$ and $ks-j\ge ks/2$ for
$0\le j\le k-2$, a direct calculation gives
\[
  \binom{u}{k-1}
  \ge (1-2(k-1)\eta)\binom{ks}{k-1}.
\]
  Using $\prod_{j=0}^{k-2}(1-j/(ks))\ge1-(k-1)(k-2)/(2ks)$ and $1/(1-a)\le1+2a$ for $0\le a\le1/2$, we obtain
  \[
    \binom n{k-1}\le\left[\left(\frac n{ks}\right)^{k-1}+\frac{2(k-1)}s\right]\binom{ks}{k-1}.
  \]
  Since $k(s+1)\le n\le(k+1/2)s$ and $s\ge2k$,
a direct calculation gives
\[
  \binom n{k-2}<\frac3s\binom{ks}{k-1}.
\]
Combining the three estimates above with $d\le2\eta ks$, we obtain
\[
  \begin{aligned}
    C_k(s)-|\mathcal H'|
    &\ge d\binom{ks}{k-1}
    \biggl[
      2-\left(\frac n{ks}\right)^{k-1}
      -\bigl(4(k-1)+6k(k-1)+3k^3\bigr)\eta\\
    &\qquad\qquad
      -\frac{2(k-1)+3k(k-1)^2}{s}
    \biggr]\\
    &\ge d\binom{ks}{k-1}
    \left[
      2-\left(\frac n{ks}\right)^{k-1}
      -5k^3\eta-\frac{3k^3}{s}
    \right].
  \end{aligned}
\]
The second inequality follows from
$4(k-1)+6k(k-1)+3k^3\le5k^3$ and
$2(k-1)+3k(k-1)^2\le3k^3$ for $k\ge3$.
  This proves \cref{fact:large-clique-deficit}.\qedhere
head: environment

label: clm:large-clique-e1-matching
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{clm:large-clique-e1-matching}
    There is no matching of size $\ell_F+1$ in $\mathcal E_1$ such that every edge meets $F$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose for a contradiction that $E_1,\ldots,E_{\ell_F+1}$ form such a matching.
    Each $E_j$ meets $B$ only in a single vertex of $F$, so it is disjoint from all the edges in $\mathcal M'\setminus\{F\}$.
    Replacing $F$ by these edges produces a matching $\widetilde{\mathcal M}=(\mathcal M'\setminus\{F\})\cup\{E_1,\ldots,E_{\ell_F+1}\}$ in $\mathcal H'$, so $|\widetilde{\mathcal M}|\le s$.
    Deleting $F$ removes $\ell_F$ vertices outside $Q$, while the new edges add at least $\ell_F+1$ distinct vertices of $W$.
    This implies $|V(\widetilde{\mathcal M})\setminus Q|\ge d+1$.
    Thus, $|Q\cup V(\widetilde{\mathcal M})|\ge u+d+1=k(s+1)$.
    Hence, we have $|Q\setminus V(\widetilde{\mathcal M})|=|Q\cup V(\widetilde{\mathcal M})|-k|\widetilde{\mathcal M}|\ge k(s+1-|\widetilde{\mathcal M}|)$.
    Choose $k(s+1-|\widetilde{\mathcal M}|)$ of these unused vertices and partition them into $s+1-|\widetilde{\mathcal M}|$ clique edges.
    Together with $\widetilde{\mathcal M}$, they form an $(s+1)$-matching in $\mathcal H'$, a contradiction.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose $0<\eta\le1/(64k^4)$, and then choose $s_0=s_0(k,\eta)$ such that $s_0\ge60k^4$ and $\eta ks_0\ge k-1$.
  Let $\mathcal H$ satisfy the hypotheses of \cref{lem:large-clique-emc}.

  Add edges to $\mathcal H$ while the matching number remains at most $s$, obtaining a maximal family $\mathcal H'$.
  Since $n\ge k(s+1)$, the family $\mathcal H'$ has a missing edge.
  By maximality, adding any missing edge creates an $(s+1)$-matching.
  Thus, $\nu(\mathcal H')=s$ and $\mathcal H'$ is $s$-saturated.
  Let $Q$ be a largest clique in $\mathcal H'$, set $u=|Q|$ and $d=ks+k-1-u$, and apply \cref{fact:large-clique-deficit}.
  Since $n/(ks)\le1+1/(2k)$, we have
  \[
    2-\left(\frac n{ks}\right)^{k-1}
    \ge2-\left(1+\frac1{2k}\right)^{k-1}
    >2-\mathrm{e}^{1/2}>0.
  \]
  By our choices of $\eta$ and $s_0$, we have $5k^3\eta+3k^3/s\le5/(64k)+1/(20k)<2-\mathrm{e}^{1/2}$.
  By \cref{fact:large-clique-deficit}, we therefore have $|\mathcal H|\le|\mathcal H'|\le C_k(s)$, with strict inequality whenever $d>0$.
  If $d=0$, then $|Q|=ks+k-1$.
  Any edge $E\in\mathcal H'$ not contained in $Q$ leaves at least $ks$ vertices of $Q$ unused.
  Partitioning $ks$ of these vertices into $s$ clique edges gives an $(s+1)$-matching together with $E$, a contradiction.
  Thus, $\mathcal H'=\binom Qk$, and equality forces $\mathcal H=\binom Qk$.
  Conversely, every clique family on $ks+k-1$ vertices has $C_k(s)$ members and satisfies the hypotheses.

label: prop:unified-stability
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:unified-stability}
  Let $k\ge3$ be an integer and let $L>k$.
  For every $\varepsilon>0$ and $\eta>0$, there exist $\delta=\delta(k,L,\varepsilon,\eta)>0$ and an integer $s_0=s_0(k,L,\varepsilon,\eta)$ such that the following holds.
  Let $n$ and $s$ be integers with $s\ge s_0$ and $k(s+1)\le n\le Ls$, and let $\mathcal F\subseteq\binom{[n]}k$ satisfy
  \[
    \nu(\mathcal F)\le s
    \text{ and }
    |\mathcal F|\ge D_k(n,s)-\delta n^k.
  \]
  Then the following hold.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item If $n\ge(\rho_k+\eta)s$, then there is an $s$-set $S\subseteq[n]$ such that $|\mathcal F\triangle\mathcal A(S)|\le\varepsilon n^k$.
    \item If $n\le(\rho_k-\eta)s$, then there is a $(ks+k-1)$-set $Q\subseteq[n]$ such that $\left|\mathcal F\triangle\binom Qk\right|\le\varepsilon n^k$.
    \item If $(\rho_k-\eta)s<n<(\rho_k+\eta)s$, then there is either an $s$-set $S\subseteq[n]$ such that $|\mathcal F\triangle\mathcal A(S)|\le\varepsilon n^k$, or a $(ks+k-1)$-set $Q\subseteq[n]$ such that $\left|\mathcal F\triangle\binom Qk\right|\le\varepsilon n^k$.
  \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose for a contradiction that \cref{prop:unified-stability} fails for some fixed $k$, $L$, $\varepsilon$ and $\eta$ as in the statement.
  Then there are integer pairs $(n_i,s_i)$ with $s_i\ge i$ and $k(s_i+1)\le n_i\le Ls_i$, and families $\mathcal F_i\subseteq\binom{[n_i]}k$ satisfying
  \[
    \nu(\mathcal F_i)\le s_i
    \text{ and }
    |\mathcal F_i|\ge D_k(n_i,s_i)-\frac{n_i^k}{i},
  \]
  such that the conclusion of \cref{prop:unified-stability} fails for every $i$.

  Since $n_i/s_i$ is bounded, after passing to a subsequence, we may assume that $n_i/s_i\to R$ for some $R\in[k,L]$.
  By \cref{lem:matching-sequence}\textup{(i)}, we have $\min\{d_B(\mathcal F_i),d_C(\mathcal F_i)\}=o(n_i^k)$.
  Since $\varepsilon>0$, for every sufficiently large $i$, at least one of these distances is at most $\varepsilon n_i^k$.
  Thus, \textup{(iii)} of \cref{prop:unified-stability} holds whenever $(\rho_k-\eta)s_i<n_i<(\rho_k+\eta)s_i$.
  Since every $\mathcal F_i$ is a counterexample, after omitting finitely many initial terms and passing to a further subsequence, we may assume that either $n_i\ge(\rho_k+\eta)s_i$ for every $i$ or $n_i\le(\rho_k-\eta)s_i$ for every $i$.
  In the first case, failure of the cover conclusion means that $d_B(\mathcal F_i)>\varepsilon n_i^k$.
  But $R\ge\rho_k+\eta>\rho_k$, so \cref{lem:matching-sequence}\textup{(ii)} implies $d_B(\mathcal F_i)=o(n_i^k)$, a contradiction.
  In the second case, failure of the clique conclusion means that $d_C(\mathcal F_i)>\varepsilon n_i^k$.
  But $k\le R\le\rho_k-\eta<\rho_k$, so \cref{lem:matching-sequence}\textup{(ii)} implies $d_C(\mathcal F_i)=o(n_i^k)$, again a contradiction.
  This proves \cref{prop:unified-stability}.

label: cor:hilton-milner
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{cor:hilton-milner}
  For every fixed integer $k\ge3$, there is an integer $s_{\mathcal{HM}}(k)$ such that, for all integers $s\ge s_{\mathcal{HM}}(k)$ and $n\ge k(s+1)$, every family $\mathcal F\subseteq\binom{[n]}k$ with $\nu(\mathcal F)\le s<\tau(\mathcal F)$ satisfies
  \[
    |\mathcal F|\le\max\{C_k(s),\mathcal{HM}_k(n,s)\}.
  \]
  Equality holds if and only if one of the following statements holds.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item $C_k(s)>\mathcal{HM}_k(n,s)$ and $\mathcal F=\binom Qk$ for some $(ks+k-1)$-set $Q\subseteq[n]$.
    \item $C_k(s)<\mathcal{HM}_k(n,s)$ and $\mathcal F\in\mathcal R_k(n,s)$.
    \item $C_k(s)=\mathcal{HM}_k(n,s)$, $\mathcal F=\binom Qk$ for some $(ks+k-1)$-set $Q\subseteq[n]$ or $\mathcal F\in\mathcal R_k(n,s)$.
  \end{enumerate}

label: lem:sparse-hm
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sparse-hm}
  Let $k\ge3$, $n\ge k$, and $b\ge1$ be integers with $b\le n/(4k^3)$.
  If $\mathcal J\subseteq\binom{[n]}k$ satisfies $\nu(\mathcal J)\le b<\tau(\mathcal J)$, then $|\mathcal J|\le\mathcal{HM}_k(n,b)$.
  Equality holds if and only if $\mathcal J\in\mathcal R_k(n,b)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $n\ge4k^3b>2k^3b$, \cref{thm:bde} implies $|\mathcal J|\le\mathcal{HM}_k(n,b)$.
  We now determine the equality cases by induction on $b$.
  When $b=1$, we have $n>2k$, so equality implies $\mathcal J\in\mathcal R_k(n,1)$ by~\cite[Theorem~1.2]{HanKohayakawa}.

  Suppose $b\ge2$, $\nu(\mathcal J)\le b<\tau(\mathcal J)$, and $|\mathcal J|=\mathcal{HM}_k(n,b)$.
  We first find a vertex $v$ with $d_{\mathcal J}(v)>kb\binom{n-2}{k-2}$, and then prove $\nu(\mathcal J-v)\le b-1$.
  To this end, let $\mathcal M$ be a maximal matching in $\mathcal J$ and set $U=\bigcup_{E\in\mathcal M}E$.
  Since $|\mathcal M|\le b$, we have $|U|=k|\mathcal M|\le kb$.
  Every edge of $\mathcal J$ meets $U$, since otherwise it could be added to $\mathcal M$, contradicting maximality.
  Thus, counting incidences between $U$ and the edges of $\mathcal J$, we obtain
  \[
    \sum_{u\in U}d_{\mathcal J}(u)
    =\sum_{E\in\mathcal J}|E\cap U|
    \ge|\mathcal J|.
  \]
  By averaging, there is a vertex $v\in U$ such that
  \[
    d_{\mathcal J}(v)\ge\frac{|\mathcal J|}{|U|}
    \ge\frac{|\mathcal J|}{kb}
    =\frac{\mathcal{HM}_k(n,b)}{kb}>\frac{b-1}{kb}\binom{n-b+1}{k-1}
    \ge\frac1{2k}\binom{n-b+1}{k-1},
  \]
  where the strict inequality follows from
  \[
    \mathcal{HM}_k(n,b)
    =\mathcal{HM}_k(n-b+1,1)+\sum_{i=1}^{b-1}\binom{n-i}{k-1},
  \]
  obtained from the definition of $\mathcal{HM}_k(n,s)$.
  Calculation shows that
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      \binom{n-b+1}{k-1}
       & =\binom{n-1}{k-1}-\sum_{i=1}^{b-2}\binom{n-i-1}{k-2}   \\
       & \ge\binom{n-1}{k-1}-(b-2)\binom{n-2}{k-2}              \\
       & =\left(1-\frac{(b-2)(k-1)}{n-1}\right)\binom{n-1}{k-1}
      \ge\frac12\binom{n-1}{k-1},
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  where the last inequality follows from $n\ge4k^3b$.
  Consequently,
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:sparse-hm-high-degree}
    d_{\mathcal J}(v)
    >\frac1{4k}\binom{n-1}{k-1}
    =\frac{n-1}{4k(k-1)}\binom{n-2}{k-2}
    >kb\binom{n-2}{k-2}.
  \end{equation}
  The last inequality follows from $n-1\ge4k^3b-1>4k^2(k-1)b$.

  Let $\mathcal J-v=\{E\in\mathcal J:v\notin E\}$.
  We claim that $\nu(\mathcal J-v)\le b-1$.
  Suppose for a contradiction that $\mathcal J-v$ contains a matching $\mathcal N$ of $b$ edges.
  Let $W=\bigcup_{E\in\mathcal N}E$.
  Then $|W|=kb$ and $v\notin W$.
  For each $w\in W$, at most $\binom{n-2}{k-2}$ edges of $\mathcal J$ contain both $v$ and $w$.
  Thus, at most $kb\binom{n-2}{k-2}$ edges of $\mathcal J$ contain $v$ and meet $W$.
  By \eqref{eq:sparse-hm-high-degree}, there exists an edge $F\in\mathcal J$ that contains $v$ and is disjoint from $W$.
  Then $\mathcal N\cup\{F\}$ is a matching of $b+1$ edges in $\mathcal J$, contradicting $\nu(\mathcal J)\le b$.
  Thus, $\nu(\mathcal J-v)\le b-1$.
  Also, $\tau(\mathcal J-v)>b-1$, since a cover of size at most $b-1$ together with $v$ would cover $\mathcal J$ with at most $b$ vertices.
  Since $n-1\ge4k^3(b-1)>2k^3(b-1)$, \cref{thm:bde} applies to $\mathcal J-v$, and hence
  \[
    |\mathcal J|
    =d_{\mathcal J}(v)+|\mathcal J-v|
    \le\binom{n-1}{k-1}+\mathcal{HM}_k(n-1,b-1)
    =\mathcal{HM}_k(n,b).
  \]
  Since $|\mathcal J|=\mathcal{HM}_k(n,b)$, equality holds throughout.
  Thus, $\mathcal J$ contains every $k$-set through $v$, and $\mathcal J-v$ attains the bound $\mathcal{HM}_k(n-1,b-1)$.
  By induction, $\mathcal J-v\in\mathcal R_k(n-1,b-1)$ after relabeling.
  Adding all $k$-sets through $v$ replaces $S_0$ by $S_0\cup\{v\}$ in the construction $\mathcal H(S_0,u,E_0)$, or in $\mathcal T(S_0,T)$ when $k=3$.
  Hence, $\mathcal J\in\mathcal R_k(n,b)$.
  Every family in $\mathcal R_k(n,b)$ attains equality, as verified in \cref{sec:hm-constructions}.
  This completes the proof.

label: cor:clique-hilton-milner
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{cor:clique-hilton-milner}
  For every fixed integer $k\ge3$ and every fixed $0<\varepsilon<\rho_k-k$, there is an integer $s_{\mathrm{cl}}(k,\varepsilon)$ such that, for all integers $s\ge s_{\mathrm{cl}}(k,\varepsilon)$ and $k(s+1)\le n\le(\rho_k-\varepsilon)s$, every family $\mathcal F\subseteq\binom{[n]}k$ with $\nu(\mathcal F)\le s$ and $|V^+(\mathcal F)|\ge k(s+1)$ satisfies
  \[
    |\mathcal F|\le\max\{J_k^{(1)}(n,s),J_k^{(2)}(n,s)\}.
  \]
  Equality holds if and only if one of the following statements holds.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item $J_k^{(1)}(n,s)>J_k^{(2)}(n,s)$ and $\mathcal F=\mathcal J_1(Q,D,v)$.
    \item $J_k^{(1)}(n,s)<J_k^{(2)}(n,s)$ and $\mathcal F=\mathcal J_2(Q,u)$.
    \item $J_k^{(1)}(n,s)=J_k^{(2)}(n,s)$ and either $\mathcal F=\mathcal J_1(Q,D,v)$ or $\mathcal F=\mathcal J_2(Q,u)$.
  \end{enumerate}

label: thm:cross-intersection
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:cross-intersection}
  Let $r\ge1$, $q\ge2r$ and $t\ge2$.
  Suppose $\mathcal L_1,\ldots,\mathcal L_t\subseteq\binom{[q]}r$ are nonempty and every member of $\mathcal L_i$ meets every member of $\mathcal L_j$ whenever $i\ne j$.
  Then
  \[
    \sum_{i=1}^t|\mathcal L_i|
    \le\max\left\{\binom qr-\binom{q-r}r+t-1,\ t\binom{q-1}{r-1}\right\}.
  \]

name: Shi--Frankl--Qian

label: thm:weighted-cross-intersection
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:weighted-cross-intersection}
  Let $k\ge3$ and $q>2(k-1)$ be integers, let $Q$ be a $q$-set, and let $c>0$.
  Suppose that $\mathcal A,\mathcal B\subseteq\binom Q{k-1}$ are nonempty, every member of $\mathcal A$ meets every member of $\mathcal B$, and $|\mathcal B|\le\binom{q-1}{k-2}$.
  Then
  \[
    |\mathcal A|+c|\mathcal B|
    \le\max\left\{\binom q{k-1}-\binom{q-k+1}{k-1}+c,\ (1+c)\binom{q-1}{k-2}\right\}.
  \]
  If equality holds, then either $\mathcal B=\{D\}$ and $\mathcal A=\{A\in\binom Q{k-1}:A\cap D\ne\emptyset\}$ for some $D\in\binom Q{k-1}$, or $\mathcal A=\mathcal B=\{A\in\binom Q{k-1}:z\in A\}$ for some $z\in Q$.

label: lem:large-clique
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:large-clique}
  For each fixed $k\ge3$, there exist $\eta>0$ and $s_0$ such that the following holds whenever $s\ge s_0$ and $k(s+1)\le n\le(k+1/2)s$.
  If $\mathcal H\subseteq\binom{[n]}k$ satisfies $\nu(\mathcal H)\le s$, $|V^+(\mathcal H)|\ge k(s+1)$, and $\omega(\mathcal H)\ge(1-\eta)ks$, then $|\mathcal H|\le J_k(n,s)$.
  Equality holds if and only if one of the following statements holds for some admissible choice of the parameters defining $\mathcal J_1$ and $\mathcal J_2$.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item $J_k^{(1)}(n,s)>J_k^{(2)}(n,s)$ and $\mathcal H=\mathcal J_1(Q,D,v)$.
    \item $J_k^{(1)}(n,s)<J_k^{(2)}(n,s)$ and $\mathcal H=\mathcal J_2(Q,u)$.
    \item $J_k^{(1)}(n,s)=J_k^{(2)}(n,s)$ and either $\mathcal H=\mathcal J_1(Q,D,v)$ or $\mathcal H=\mathcal J_2(Q,u)$.
  \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose $0<\eta=\eta(k)\le1/(64k^4)$ sufficiently small for the estimates in Case~2, and then choose $s_0=s_0(k,\eta)\ge60k^4$ sufficiently large that $\eta ks_0\ge k-1$ and the estimates below hold.
  Recall that $q=ks+k-2$ and $t=n-q\ge2$.

  Extend $\mathcal H$ to an $s$-saturated family $\mathcal H'$.
  Let $Q$ be a largest clique in $\mathcal H'$.
  Write $u$ for the order of $Q$.
  Since $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal H'$, we have $u\ge\omega(\mathcal H)\ge(1-\eta)ks$.
  If $u\ge q+2=k(s+1)$, then a partition of $k(s+1)$ vertices of $Q$ into $s+1$ sets of size $k$ forms an $(s+1)$-matching in $\mathcal H'$, contradicting $\nu(\mathcal H')=s$.
  Thus, $u\le q+1$.
  If $u=q+1$, then the condition $|V^+(\mathcal H)|\ge q+2$ ensures that there is an edge $E\in\mathcal H$ not contained in $Q$.
  Since $|Q\setminus E|\ge q+1-(k-1)=ks$, we can choose $s$ pairwise disjoint $k$-sets in $Q\setminus E$.
  Together with $E$, they form an $(s+1)$-matching in $\mathcal H'$, a contradiction.
  Hence, $(1-\eta)ks\le u\le q$.
  We now consider two cases according to the value of $u$.

  \medskip
  \noindent{\bf Case 1.} $u=q$.
  \medskip

  In this case, we claim that every edge of $\mathcal H'$ not contained in $Q$ has exactly one vertex outside $Q$.
  Indeed, an edge $E\in\mathcal H'$ containing at least two vertices outside $Q$ would leave at least $q-(k-2)=ks$ vertices of $Q$ unused.
  Choose $s$ pairwise disjoint $k$-sets among these vertices.
  Together with $E$, they form an $(s+1)$-matching in $\mathcal H'$, a contradiction.

  For each $v\in[n]\setminus Q$, define
  \[
    \mathcal L_v=\left\{A\in\binom Q{k-1}:A\cup\{v\}\in\mathcal H'\right\}.
  \]
  For distinct $v,w\in[n]\setminus Q$, we have $A\cap B\ne\emptyset$ for all $A\in\mathcal L_v$ and $B\in\mathcal L_w$.
  Otherwise, disjoint $A\in\mathcal L_v$ and $B\in\mathcal L_w$ would extend to two disjoint edges $\{v\}\cup A$ and $\{w\}\cup B$ of $\mathcal H'$.
  The remaining $q-2(k-1)=k(s-1)$ vertices of $Q$ can be partitioned into $s-1$ clique edges, completing an $(s+1)$-matching in $\mathcal H'$, a contradiction.

  Let $t'$ be the number of vertices $v\in[n]\setminus Q$ for which $\mathcal L_v\ne\emptyset$.
  We have $t'\ge2$, since otherwise $|V^+(\mathcal H)|\le q+1$.
  The $t'$ nonempty families $\mathcal L_v\subseteq\binom Q{k-1}$ satisfy the hypotheses of \cref{thm:cross-intersection}, since $q\ge2(k-1)$.
  Since $Q$ is a clique and every edge of $\mathcal H'$ outside $Q$ is counted by exactly one link, \cref{thm:cross-intersection} implies
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      |\mathcal H|
       & \le|\mathcal H'|=\binom qk+\sum_{v\in[n]\setminus Q}|\mathcal L_v|                         \\
       & \le\binom qk+\max\left\{\binom q{k-1}-\binom{q-k+1}{k-1}+t'-1,\ t'\binom{q-1}{k-2}\right\} \\
       & \le J_k(n,s),
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  where the last inequality uses $t'\le t$ and the definition of $J_k(n,s)$.
  This proves the upper bound in this case.

  We now characterize the equality cases.
  Suppose that $|\mathcal H|=J_k(n,s)$.
  Equality holds throughout the bound on $|\mathcal H|$, so $\mathcal H=\mathcal H'$ and $t'=t$.
  In particular, $\mathcal L_x$ is nonempty for every $x\in[n]\setminus Q$.
  Choose distinct $v,w\in[n]\setminus Q$ whose links have the largest and second largest sizes, respectively.

  To apply \cref{thm:weighted-cross-intersection} to $\mathcal L_v$ and $\mathcal L_w$, we first show that $|\mathcal L_w|\le\binom{q-1}{k-2}$.
  Suppose otherwise and choose $\mathcal B\subseteq\mathcal L_w$ with $|\mathcal B|=\binom{q-1}{k-2}$.
  Every member of $\mathcal L_v$ meets every member of $\mathcal B$, and $q=ks+k-2>2(k-1)$ for $s\ge2$.
  Thus, \cref{thm:weighted-cross-intersection} applies to $\mathcal L_v$ and $\mathcal B$.
  Since $\binom{q-1}{k-2}>1$, for sufficiently large $c$ we have
  \[
    (1+c)\binom{q-1}{k-2}
    >\binom q{k-1}-\binom{q-k+1}{k-1}+c.
  \]
  Hence, \cref{thm:weighted-cross-intersection} gives
  \[
    |\mathcal L_v|+c\binom{q-1}{k-2}
    \le(1+c)\binom{q-1}{k-2}.
  \]
  Hence, $|\mathcal L_v|\le\binom{q-1}{k-2}$, contradicting $|\mathcal L_v|\ge|\mathcal L_w|>\binom{q-1}{k-2}$.
  Thus, $|\mathcal L_w|\le\binom{q-1}{k-2}$.

  To determine the possible forms of the two largest links, we show that $(\mathcal L_v,\mathcal L_w)$ attains equality in \cref{thm:weighted-cross-intersection}.
  By the choice of $w$, each of the $t-1$ links other than $\mathcal L_v$ has size at most $|\mathcal L_w|$.
  Hence, by \cref{thm:weighted-cross-intersection},
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      J_k(n,s)-\binom qk
       & =|\mathcal H|-\binom qk \\
       & =\sum_{x\in[n]\setminus Q}|\mathcal L_x| \\
       & \le|\mathcal L_v|+(t-1)|\mathcal L_w| \\
       & \le\max\left\{\binom q{k-1}-\binom{q-k+1}{k-1}+t-1,\ t\binom{q-1}{k-2}\right\} \\
       & =J_k(n,s)-\binom qk.
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  Thus, both inequalities are equalities.
  The first implies that $|\mathcal L_x|=|\mathcal L_w|$ for every $x\in[n]\setminus(Q\cup\{v\})$.
  By \cref{thm:weighted-cross-intersection}, the second implies that one of the following statements holds.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item $\mathcal L_w=\{D\}$ and $\mathcal L_v=\{A\in\binom Q{k-1}:A\cap D\ne\emptyset\}$ for some $D\in\binom Q{k-1}$.
    \item $\mathcal L_v=\mathcal L_w=\{A\in\binom Q{k-1}:z\in A\}$ for some $z\in Q$.
  \end{enumerate}

  If \textup{(i)} holds, then we show that $\mathcal L_x=\{D\}$ for every $x\in[n]\setminus(Q\cup\{v\})$.
  Fix such an $x$ and suppose that $B\ne D$ for some $B\in\mathcal L_x$.
  Since $|B|=|D|$, we can choose some $d\in D\setminus B$.
  As $q>2(k-1)$, there is a $(k-1)$-set $A\subseteq Q\setminus B$ containing $d$.
  Since $d\in A\cap D$, the set $A$ meets $D$ and therefore belongs to $\mathcal L_v$ by \textup{(i)}.
  However, $A\subseteq Q\setminus B$ implies $A\cap B=\emptyset$, contradicting the fact that every member of $\mathcal L_v$ meets every member of $\mathcal L_x$.
  Thus, no member of $\mathcal L_x$ can differ from $D$.
  Since $x$ was arbitrary and each of these links is nonempty, $\mathcal L_x=\{D\}$ for every $x\in[n]\setminus(Q\cup\{v\})$.
  Recall that every edge of $\mathcal H$ not contained in $Q$ has exactly one vertex outside $Q$.
  By \textup{(i)}, the edges containing $v$ are precisely the sets $\{v\}\cup A$ with $A\in\binom Q{k-1}$ and $A\cap D\ne\emptyset$.
  For each $x\in[n]\setminus(Q\cup\{v\})$, the equality $\mathcal L_x=\{D\}$ means that the only edge containing $x$ is $\{x\}\cup D$.
  Since $\mathcal H$ also contains all $k$-subsets of $Q$, we have $\mathcal H=\mathcal J_1(Q,D,v)$.

  If \textup{(ii)} holds, then $\mathcal L_v$ consists of all $(k-1)$-subsets of $Q$ containing $z$.
  Fix $x\in[n]\setminus(Q\cup\{v\})$ and take any $B\in\mathcal L_x$.
  Since $B$ meets every member of $\mathcal L_v$, it must meet every $(k-1)$-subset of $Q$ containing $z$.
  We show that this forces $z\in B$.
  Suppose otherwise.
  Since $z\in Q\setminus B$ and $q>2(k-1)$, there is a $(k-1)$-set $A\subseteq Q\setminus B$ containing $z$.
  This set contains $z$ but is disjoint from $B$, contradicting the fact that $B$ meets every $(k-1)$-subset of $Q$ containing $z$.
  Thus, every member of $\mathcal L_x$ contains $z$, so $\mathcal L_x\subseteq\mathcal L_v$.
  We already concluded that $|\mathcal L_x|=|\mathcal L_w|$, and \textup{(ii)} states that $\mathcal L_w=\mathcal L_v$, so $\mathcal L_x=\mathcal L_v$.
  Therefore, for every $x\in[n]\setminus Q$, the edges containing $x$ are precisely the sets $\{x\}\cup A$ with $A\in\binom Q{k-1}$ and $z\in A$.
  Since $\mathcal H$ also contains all $k$-subsets of $Q$, we have $\mathcal H=\mathcal J_2(Q,z)$.

  Among $\mathcal J_1(Q,D,v)$ and $\mathcal J_2(Q,z)$, only those attaining the maximum defining $J_k(n,s)$ can occur, since $|\mathcal H|=J_k(n,s)$.
  This finishes the proof of Case 1.

  \medskip
  \noindent{\bf Case 2.} $(1-\eta)ks\le u\le q-1$.
  \medskip

  In this case, we show that $|\mathcal H'|<J_k^{(2)}(n,s)$.
  Set $d=q+1-u\ge2$ and $x=(k-1)(n/(ks)-1)$.
  Since $k(s+1)\le n\le(k+1/2)s$, we have $0\le x\le(k-1)/(2k)<1/2$.
  Since $q=ks+k-2$ and $t=n-ks-k+2$, we obtain $J_k^{(2)}(n,s)-C_k(s)=t\binom{q-1}{k-2}-\binom q{k-1}$ from Pascal's identity.
  For $s\ge2k$, we have $\binom{q-1}{k-2}\ge\binom{ks}{k-2}$.
  By the product formula, $\binom{ks+k-3}{k-2}<2\binom{ks}{k-2}<4\binom{ks}{k-1}/s$.
  Therefore, Pascal's identity yields
  \[
    \binom q{k-1}-\binom{ks}{k-1}
    =\sum_{j=1}^{k-2}\binom{ks+j-1}{k-2}
    <\frac{4k}{s}\binom{ks}{k-1}.
  \]
  As $t=n-ks-k+2$ and $\binom{ks}{k-2}/\binom{ks}{k-1}=(k-1)/(ks-k+2)$, we also have
  \[
    \frac{t\binom{q-1}{k-2}}{\binom{ks}{k-1}}
    \ge\frac{t(k-1)}{ks}
    =x-\frac{(k-1)(k-2)}{ks}
    \ge x-\frac{k-1}{s}.
  \]
  Consequently,
  \[
    \frac{J_k^{(2)}(n,s)-C_k(s)}{\binom{ks}{k-1}}
    \ge-1+x-\frac{5k}{s}.
  \]
  \Cref{fact:large-clique-deficit} applies to the $s$-saturated family $\mathcal H'$ with $d=q+1-u$.
  Since $(n/(ks))^{k-1}\le\mathrm{e}^x$ and $5k^3\eta+3k^3/s\le5/(64k)+1/(20k)<2-\mathrm{e}^{1/2}$, the quantity $2-(n/(ks))^{k-1}-5k^3\eta-3k^3/s$ is positive.
  Using $d\ge2$ and $\mathrm{e}^x\le1+x+x^2$ for $x\le1/2$, we obtain
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      \frac{J_k^{(2)}(n,s)-|\mathcal H'|}{\binom{ks}{k-1}}
       & \ge d\left[2-\left(\frac n{ks}\right)^{k-1}-5k^3\eta-\frac{3k^3}s\right]
      -1+x-\frac{5k}s                                                             \\
       & \ge 3-2\mathrm{e}^x+x-10k^3\eta-\frac{6k^3+5k}s                          \\
       & \ge (1-2x)(1+x)-10k^3\eta-\frac{6k^3+5k}s                                \\
       & \ge\frac1k-10k^3\eta-\frac{6k^3+5k}s>0.
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  Indeed, $x\le(k-1)/(2k)$ implies $(1-2x)(1+x)\ge1/k$, while $10k^3\eta+(6k^3+5k)/s\le5/(32k)+1/(10k)+1/(12k^3)<1/k$.
  Hence, $|\mathcal H|\le|\mathcal H'|<J_k^{(2)}(n,s)\le J_k(n,s)$.
  Equality can therefore occur only in Case~1.

  \medskip
  This completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $k\ge3$ and $0<\varepsilon<\rho_k-k$, and set $R=\rho_k-\varepsilon$, so $k<R<\rho_k<k+1/2$.
  We first consider families without isolated vertices.
  We show that, for all sufficiently large $s$ and $k(s+1)\le n\le Rs$, any such family $\mathcal F\subseteq\binom{[n]}k$ satisfying $\nu(\mathcal F)\le s$ and $|\mathcal F|\ge J_k(n,s)$ equals $\mathcal J_1(Q,D,v)$ or $\mathcal J_2(Q,u)$ for a choice of parameters giving size $J_k(n,s)$.
  This will establish both the upper bound and its equality cases for families without isolated vertices.
  We will then delete isolated vertices to obtain the full statement.

  Suppose that the assertion for families without isolated vertices fails for arbitrarily large $s$.
  Choose a sequence of counterexamples $\mathcal F_i\subseteq\binom{[n_i]}k$ with $s_i\to\infty$ and $k(s_i+1)\le n_i\le Rs_i$.
  Each $\mathcal F_i$ has no isolated vertices, satisfies $\nu(\mathcal F_i)\le s_i$, and has
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:support-counterexample-sequence}
    |\mathcal F_i|\ge J_k(n_i,s_i),
  \end{equation}
  but equals neither $\mathcal J_1(Q,D,v)$ nor $\mathcal J_2(Q,u)$ for any choice of parameters giving size $J_k(n_i,s_i)$.

  Ordinary shifts may create isolated vertices, so we restrict ourselves to shifts that preserve the absence of isolated vertices.
  For a family $\mathcal H$, set $\mathcal D(\mathcal H)=\sum_v d_{\mathcal H}(v)^2$.
  For each $i$, start with $\mathcal H=\mathcal F_i$.
  Whenever there exists an ordered pair of distinct vertices $(u,v)$ satisfying $d_{S_{uv}(\mathcal H)}(v)>0$ and $\mathcal D(S_{uv}(\mathcal H))>\mathcal D(\mathcal H)$, choose one such pair and replace $\mathcal H$ by $S_{uv}(\mathcal H)$.
  Only the degree of $v$ can decrease under $S_{uv}$, so $d_{S_{uv}(\mathcal H)}(v)>0$ ensures that no vertex becomes isolated.
  Repeat this step until no ordered pair satisfies both conditions, and denote the resulting family by $\mathcal G_i$.
  The process terminates because $\mathcal D$ takes integer values and is bounded above on the finite set of families on $[n_i]$.
  By our choice of shifts, every family along the sequence has $|\mathcal F_i|$ edges, no isolated vertices, and matching number at most $s_i$.

  Passing to a subsequence and relabeling, we may assume that
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:support-limiting-ratio}
    n_i/s_i\longrightarrow R_*\in[k,R].
  \end{equation}
  Since $R_*<\rho_k$, we have $(k/R_*)^k>1-(1-1/R_*)^k$.
  Thus, \eqref{eq:support-limiting-ratio} and \cref{fact:construction-densities} imply $D_k(n_i,s_i)=C_k(s_i)$ for all sufficiently large $i$.
  Also, the formulas for $J_k^{(1)}(n,s)$ and $J_k^{(2)}(n,s)$ imply $J_k(n,s)=C_k(s)+O_k(s^{k-1})$ uniformly for $k(s+1)\le n\le Rs$.
  Since $n_i=\Theta_k(s_i)$, \eqref{eq:support-counterexample-sequence} implies
  \[
    |\mathcal G_i|=|\mathcal F_i|
    \ge D_k(n_i,s_i)-O_k(s_i^{k-1})
    =D_k(n_i,s_i)-o(n_i^k).
  \]
  By \cref{lem:matching-sequence}\textup{(ii)}, there are $(ks_i+k-1)$-sets $Q_i\subseteq[n_i]$ such that
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:support-clique-approximation}
    \left|\mathcal G_i\triangle\binom{Q_i}k\right|=o(n_i^k)=o(s_i^k).
  \end{equation}

  Let $0<\eta<1$ be the constant supplied by \cref{lem:large-clique}.
  The following claim shows that the approximation in \eqref{eq:support-clique-approximation} yields a clique large enough to apply \cref{lem:large-clique}.

  \begin{claim}\label{lem:support-preserving-compression}
    For all sufficiently large $i$, we have $\omega(\mathcal G_i)\ge(1-\eta)ks_i$.
  \end{claim}

  \begin{proof}
    Set $\Delta_i=\binom{ks_i+k-2}{k-1}$, and let
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:high-core-degrees}
      T_i=\left\{v\in Q_i:d_{\mathcal G_i}(v)>\frac12\binom{n_i-2}{k-1}\right\}.
    \end{equation}
    We first show that $|Q_i\setminus T_i|=o(s_i)$.
    A short calculation shows that
    \[
      \frac{\Delta_i}{\binom{n_i-2}{k-1}}
      =\prod_{j=0}^{k-2}\frac{ks_i+k-2-j}{n_i-2-j}.
    \]
    Every numerator is at least $ks_i$ and every denominator is at most $n_i$, so each factor is at least $ks_i/n_i\ge2k/(2k+1)$.
    By Bernoulli's inequality $(1-t)^{k-1}\ge1-(k-1)t$ for $0\le t\le1$, we therefore have
    \[
      \frac{\Delta_i}{\binom{n_i-2}{k-1}}
      \ge\left(1-\frac1{2k+1}\right)^{k-1}
      \ge1-\frac{k-1}{2k+1}
      =\frac{k+2}{2k+1}>\frac12.
    \]
    For $n_i\ge k(s_i+1)$, a similar argument shows that $\binom{n_i-2}{k-1}\ge(ks_i)^{k-1}/(k-1)!$.
    Hence, $\Delta_i-\frac12\binom{n_i-2}{k-1}=\Omega_k(s_i^{k-1})$.
    Each vertex $v\in Q_i\setminus T_i$ lies in $\Delta_i$ members of $\binom{Q_i}k$, of which at most $d_{\mathcal G_i}(v)\le\frac12\binom{n_i-2}{k-1}$ belong to $\mathcal G_i$.
    Thus, at least $\Delta_i-\frac12\binom{n_i-2}{k-1}$ of these members are missing.
    Summing the missing-member counts over $v\in Q_i\setminus T_i$ counts each missing member at most $k$ times, once for each of its vertices in $Q_i\setminus T_i$.
    Together with \eqref{eq:support-clique-approximation}, this implies
    \[
      |Q_i\setminus T_i|\left(\Delta_i-\frac12\binom{n_i-2}{k-1}\right)
      \le k\left|\binom{Q_i}k\setminus\mathcal G_i\right|
      =o(s_i^k).
    \]
    Hence, $|T_i|=ks_i+k-1-o(s_i)$.

    Order the vertices of $T_i$ as $v_1,\ldots,v_{|T_i|}$ in nonincreasing order of their degrees in $\mathcal G_i$.
    Fix distinct $u,v\in T_i$ with $u$ preceding $v$ in this order.
    If $S_{uv}$ made $v$ isolated, then no member of $\mathcal G_i$ could contain both $u$ and $v$, and no $(k-1)$-set $A\subseteq[n_i]\setminus\{u,v\}$ could have both $A\cup\{u\}$ and $A\cup\{v\}$ in $\mathcal G_i$.
    Otherwise, in either case, a member containing $v$ would remain unchanged under $S_{uv}$ by the definition of shifting.
    These two exclusions would imply $d_{\mathcal G_i}(u)+d_{\mathcal G_i}(v)\le\binom{n_i-2}{k-1}$, contrary to \eqref{eq:high-core-degrees}.
    Thus, $S_{uv}$ creates no isolated vertex.
    Let $a$ be the number of members moved by $S_{uv}$.
    If $a>0$, then
    \[
      \mathcal D(S_{uv}(\mathcal G_i))-\mathcal D(\mathcal G_i)
      =2a(d_{\mathcal G_i}(u)-d_{\mathcal G_i}(v))+2a^2>0.
    \]
    Since $d_{S_{uv}(\mathcal G_i)}(v)>0$, the construction of $\mathcal G_i$ gives $\mathcal D(S_{uv}(\mathcal G_i))\le\mathcal D(\mathcal G_i)$, a contradiction.
    Therefore, $a=0$, so $S_{uv}(\mathcal G_i)=\mathcal G_i$ whenever $u$ precedes $v$ in $T_i$.

    Set $h_i=\lceil(1-\eta)ks_i\rceil$.
    For all sufficiently large $i$, we have $h_i\le|T_i|$ and may set $U_i=\{v_1,\ldots,v_{h_i}\}$.
    Since $T_i\subseteq Q_i$, we have
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:dense-high-degree-core}
      \left|\binom{T_i}k\setminus\mathcal G_i\right|
      \le\left|\binom{Q_i}k\setminus\mathcal G_i\right|
      =o(s_i^k).
    \end{equation}
    Also, $|T_i\setminus U_i|=\eta ks_i+o(s_i)$, so $\binom{|T_i\setminus U_i|}{k}=\Theta_{k,\eta}(s_i^k)$.
    By \eqref{eq:dense-high-degree-core}, for each sufficiently large $i$ choose a member $B\in\mathcal G_i\cap\binom{T_i\setminus U_i}k$.
    Fix an arbitrary set $A\in\binom{U_i}k$.
    Now we show that $A\in \mathcal G_i$.
    To this end, write $A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_k\}$ and $B=\{b_1,\ldots,b_k\}$.
    Since $A\subseteq U_i$ and $B\subseteq T_i\setminus U_i$, the sets $A,B$ are disjoint and every vertex of $A$ precedes every vertex of $B$ in the ordering of $T_i$.
    For $0\le j\le k$, set
    \[
      B_j=\{a_1,\ldots,a_j,b_{j+1},\ldots,b_k\}.
    \]
    We have $B_0=B\in\mathcal G_i$ and $B_k=A$.
    Suppose that $1\le j\le k$ and $B_{j-1}\in\mathcal G_i$.
    Since $b_j\in B_{j-1}$ and $a_j\notin B_{j-1}$, if $B_j\notin\mathcal G_i$, then $S_{a_jb_j}$ would replace $B_{j-1}$ by $B_j$.
    This would contradict $S_{a_jb_j}(\mathcal G_i)=\mathcal G_i$, which holds because $a_j$ precedes $b_j$ in $T_i$.
    Thus, $B_j\in\mathcal G_i$, and induction shows that $A=B_k\in\mathcal G_i$.
    Since $A$ was arbitrary, $U_i$ is a clique of order $h_i\ge(1-\eta)ks_i$.
  \end{proof}

  Since $\mathcal G_i$ has no isolated vertices, $|V^+(\mathcal G_i)|=n_i\ge k(s_i+1)$.
  For all sufficiently large $i$, \cref{lem:support-preserving-compression,lem:large-clique} therefore imply
  \[
    J_k(n_i,s_i)\le|\mathcal F_i|=|\mathcal G_i|\le J_k(n_i,s_i).
  \]
  Equality holds throughout.
  Since shifts preserve the number of members, every family along the sequence of shifts from $\mathcal F_i$ to $\mathcal G_i$ has exactly $J_k(n_i,s_i)$ members.
  The equality case of \cref{lem:large-clique} shows that $\mathcal G_i$ is one of the constructions $\mathcal J_1$ and $\mathcal J_2$ attaining $J_k(n_i,s_i)$ and hence contains a clique on $q_i=ks_i+k-2$ vertices.

  It remains to transfer the equality classification from $\mathcal G_i$ back to $\mathcal F_i$ along the chosen shift sequence.
  Fix any sufficiently large $i$ such that $q_i-2\ge(1-\eta)ks_i$.
  We now argue backwards along the shift sequence for this fixed $i$.
  For the initial step, we have already shown that $\mathcal G_i$ contains a clique on $q_i$ vertices.
  For the induction step, consider two consecutive families $\mathcal K,\mathcal K'$ in the shift sequence, where $\mathcal K'=S_{uv}(\mathcal K)$.
  Assume inductively that $\mathcal K'$ contains a clique on a $q_i$-set $Q$.
  We show that the preceding family $\mathcal K$ satisfies an equality case of \cref{lem:large-clique}, which will also establish the existence of a clique on $q_i$ vertices in $\mathcal K$.
  A shift does not change membership of any $k$-set avoiding both $u$ and $v$, so $\binom{Q\setminus\{u,v\}}k\subseteq\mathcal K$.
  Hence,
  \[
    \omega(\mathcal K)\ge q_i-2=ks_i+k-4\ge(1-\eta)ks_i.
  \]

  The family $\mathcal K$ has no isolated vertices, satisfies $\nu(\mathcal K)\le s_i$, and has $|\mathcal K|=J_k(n_i,s_i)$.
  \Cref{lem:large-clique} again shows that $\mathcal K$ is one of the constructions $\mathcal J_1$ and $\mathcal J_2$ attaining $J_k(n_i,s_i)$ and, in particular, contains a clique on $q_i$ vertices.
  This completes the backward induction, so $\mathcal F_i$ is one of the constructions $\mathcal J_1$ and $\mathcal J_2$ attaining $J_k(n_i,s_i)$, a contradiction.
  This proves the bound and equality classification for families without isolated vertices.

  It remains to extend these conclusions to families with isolated vertices.
  Let $\mathcal F\subseteq\binom{[n]}k$ satisfy the hypotheses of \cref{cor:clique-hilton-milner}, and set $n'=|V^+(\mathcal F)|$.
  Delete its isolated vertices and relabel the remaining vertices to obtain a family $\mathcal F'\subseteq\binom{[n']}k$ with no isolated vertices.
  Deleting isolated vertices and relabeling preserve both the number of members and the matching number, so $\nu(\mathcal F')\le s$ and $|\mathcal F'|=|\mathcal F|$.
  For fixed $k,s$, $J_k^{(1)}(n,s)$ and $J_k^{(2)}(n,s)$ strictly increase with $n$, so their maximum $J_k(n,s)$ does as well.
  Since $k(s+1)\le n'\le n\le Rs$, the case without isolated vertices gives $|\mathcal F'|\le J_k(n',s)$, and hence
  \[
    |\mathcal F|=|\mathcal F'|\le J_k(n',s)\le J_k(n,s).
  \]
  Equality forces $n'=n$, so $\mathcal F$ has no isolated vertices and is one of the constructions $\mathcal J_1$ and $\mathcal J_2$ attaining $J_k(n,s)$.

      =o(s_i^k).
    \]
    Hence, $|T_i|=ks_i+k-1-o(s_i)$.

    Order the vertices of $T_i$ as $v_1,\ldots,v_{|T_i|}$ in nonincreasing order of their degrees in $\mathcal G_i$.
    Fix distinct $u,v\in T_i$ with $u$ preceding $v$ in this order.
    If $S_{uv}$ made $v$ isolated, then no member of $\mathcal G_i$ could contain both $u$ and $v$, and no $(k-1)$-set $A\subseteq[n_i]\setminus\{u,v\}$ could have both $A\cup\{u\}$ and $A\cup\{v\}$ in $\mathcal G_i$.
    Otherwise, in either case, a member containing $v$ would remain unchanged under $S_{uv}$ by the definition of shifting.
    These two exclusions would imply $d_{\mathcal G_i}(u)+d_{\mathcal G_i}(v)\le\binom{n_i-2}{k-1}$, contrary to \eqref{eq:high-core-degrees}.
    Thus, $S_{uv}$ creates no isolated vertex.
    Let $a$ be the number of members moved by $S_{uv}$.
    If $a>0$, then
    \[
      \mathcal D(S_{uv}(\mathcal G_i))-\mathcal D(\mathcal G_i)
      =2a(d_{\mathcal G_i}(u)-d_{\mathcal G_i}(v))+2a^2>0.
    \]
    Since $d_{S_{uv}(\mathcal G_i)}(v)>0$, the construction of $\mathcal G_i$ gives $\mathcal D(S_{uv}(\mathcal G_i))\le\mathcal D(\mathcal G_i)$, a contradiction.
    Therefore, $a=0$, so $S_{uv}(\mathcal G_i)=\mathcal G_i$ whenever $u$ precedes $v$ in $T_i$.

    Set $h_i=\lceil(1-\eta)ks_i\rceil$.
    For all sufficiently large $i$, we have $h_i\le|T_i|$ and may set $U_i=\{v_1,\ldots,v_{h_i}\}$.
    Since $T_i\subseteq Q_i$, we have
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:dense-high-degree-core}
      \left|\binom{T_i}k\setminus\mathcal G_i\right|
      \le\left|\binom{Q_i}k\setminus\mathcal G_i\right|
      =o(s_i^k).
    \end{equation}
    Also, $|T_i\setminus U_i|=\eta ks_i+o(s_i)$, so $\binom{|T_i\setminus U_i|}{k}=\Theta_{k,\eta}(s_i^k)$.
    By \eqref{eq:dense-high-degree-core}, for each sufficiently large $i$ choose a member $B\in\mathcal G_i\cap\binom{T_i\setminus U_i}k$.
    Fix an arbitrary set $A\in\binom{U_i}k$.
    Now we show that $A\in \mathcal G_i$.
    To this end, write $A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_k\}$ and $B=\{b_1,\ldots,b_k\}$.
    Since $A\subseteq U_i$ and $B\subseteq T_i\setminus U_i$, the sets $A,B$ are disjoint and every vertex of $A$ precedes every vertex of $B$ in the ordering of $T_i$.
    For $0\le j\le k$, set
    \[
      B_j=\{a_1,\ldots,a_j,b_{j+1},\ldots,b_k\}.
    \]
    We have $B_0=B\in\mathcal G_i$ and $B_k=A$.
    Suppose that $1\le j\le k$ and $B_{j-1}\in\mathcal G_i$.
    Since $b_j\in B_{j-1}$ and $a_j\notin B_{j-1}$, if $B_j\notin\mathcal G_i$, then $S_{a_jb_j}$ would replace $B_{j-1}$ by $B_j$.
    This would contradict $S_{a_jb_j}(\mathcal G_i)=\mathcal G_i$, which holds because $a_j$ precedes $b_j$ in $T_i$.
    Thus, $B_j\in\mathcal G_i$, and induction shows that $A=B_k\in\mathcal G_i$.
    Since $A$ was arbitrary, $U_i$ is a clique of order $h_i\ge(1-\eta)ks_i$.

label: lem:log-power-curvature
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:log-power-curvature}
  Let $z\in\mathbb R$, $C>z^2/4$, and $T>0$.
  Define
  \[
    f_z(t)=\frac{\log(1+zt+Ct^2)}t\text{ for }t>0, \text{ and }f_z(0)=z.
  \]
  Write $\beta_z^2=C-z^2/4$.
  The following statements hold.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item The function $f_z$ has continuous derivatives of all orders on $[0,\infty)$ with
          \[
            f_z'(0)=C-z^2/2 \text{, }f_z''(0)=2z(z^2/3-C) \text{ and }
            f_z'''(0) =-3z^4/2+6Cz^2-3C^2.
          \]
    \item If $z>0$ and $\beta_z^2<(z/2+Cts)^2<3\beta_z^2$ for all $(t,s)\in[0,T]\times[0,1]$, then $0<f_z'''(t)\le3C^2$ for $0\le t\le T$.
    \item If $z<0$ and $(z/2+Cts)^2>6\beta_z^2$ for all $(t,s)\in[0,T]\times[0,1]$, then $0<-f_z'''(t)\le\frac{-f_z'''(0)}{(1+zT+CT^2)^2}$ for $0\le t\le T$.
  \end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $B(v)=1+zv+Cv^2$ and $L(v)=\log B(v)$.
  Since $C>z^2/4$, we have $B(v)\ge1-z^2/(4C)>0$ for every $v\in\mathbb R$.
  Since $L(0)=0$, we have $f_z(t)=\int_0^1L'(ts)\,\mathrm{d} s$ for $t>0$.
  At $t=0$, the integral equals $L'(0)=z=f_z(0)$.
  Since $L$ is smooth on $\mathbb R$, all derivatives of $L'(ts)$ with respect to $t$ are continuous and bounded on $[-M,M]\times[0,1]$ for every $M>0$.
  Differentiating under the integral sign, we obtain
  \[
    f_z^{(j)}(t)=\int_0^1s^jL^{(j+1)}(ts)\,\mathrm{d} s
  \]
  for every integer $j\ge0$ and every $t\ge0$.
  In particular, $f_z$ has continuous derivatives of all orders on $[0,\infty)$.
  At zero, we have $f_z^{(j)}(0)=L^{(j+1)}(0)/(j+1)$.
  Direct differentiation yields
  \[
    L''(0)=2C-z^2 \text{, }
    L'''(0)=2z^3-6Cz \text{ and }
    L^{(4)}(0)=-6z^4+24Cz^2-12C^2.
  \]
  This proves \textup{(i)}.

  To prove \textup{(ii)} and \textup{(iii)}, define
  \[
    \xi(v)=\frac{(z/2+Cv)^2-\beta_z^2}{(z/2+Cv)^2+\beta_z^2}
    =1-\frac{2\beta_z^2}{CB(v)}.
  \]
  Since $B''=2C$ and $B'''=0$, differentiation yields
  \[
    L''=-\frac{2C\xi}{B} \text{ and }
    L^{(4)}=\frac{12C^2}{B^2}-6(L'')^2
    =\frac{12C^2}{B^2}(1-2\xi^2).
  \]
  Hence,
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:log-power-third-derivative}
    f_z'''(t)=12C^2\int_0^1
    \frac{s^3\bigl(1-2\xi(ts)^2\bigr)}{B(ts)^2}\,\mathrm{d} s.
  \end{equation}

  Under the hypotheses of \textup{(ii)}, we have $B(v)\ge1$ and $0<\xi(v)<1/2$ for $0\le v\le T$.
  By \eqref{eq:log-power-third-derivative}, for $0\le t\le T$ we obtain
  \[
    0<f_z'''(t)\le12C^2\int_0^1s^3\,\mathrm{d} s=3C^2.
  \]
  This proves \textup{(ii)}.

  Under the hypotheses of \textup{(iii)}, we have $(z/2+Cv)^2>6\beta_z^2>0$, so $z/2+Cv\ne0$ for $0\le v\le T$.
  Since $z/2<0$ and $v\mapsto z/2+Cv$ is continuous, the intermediate value theorem implies $z/2+Cv<0$ for $0\le v\le T$.
  Thus, $B'(v)=z+2Cv<0$, and $\xi(v)=1-2\beta_z^2/(CB(v))$ also decreases with $v$.
  Since $5/7<\xi(v)<1$, we have $0<2\xi(v)^2-1\le2\xi(0)^2-1$ for $0\le v\le T$.
  Using $B(ts)\ge B(T)>0$ and $2\xi(ts)^2-1\le2\xi(0)^2-1$ in \eqref{eq:log-power-third-derivative}, for $0\le t\le T$ we obtain
  \[
    0<-f_z'''(t)
    \le\frac{3C^2\bigl(2\xi(0)^2-1\bigr)}{B(T)^2}
    =\frac{-f_z'''(0)}{(1+zT+CT^2)^2},
  \]
  proving \textup{(iii)}.

label: eq:crossing-gamma-bounds
title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that $\gamma=-\log(1-\mathrm{e}^{-1})$.
  Set $C=41/500$, $T=1/5$, and $\rho=37/100$.
  Write $g_-=45867/100000$ and $g_+=11467/25000$.
  The alternating Taylor bounds for the exponential imply
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      \mathrm{e}^{-g_-}+\mathrm{e}^{-1}
       & >\sum_{j=0}^{7}\frac{(-g_-)^j}{j!}
      +\sum_{j=0}^{9}\frac{(-1)^j}{j!}>1,   \\
      \mathrm{e}^{-g_+}+\mathrm{e}^{-1}
       & <\sum_{j=0}^{8}\frac{(-g_+)^j}{j!}
      +\sum_{j=0}^{12}\frac{(-1)^j}{j!}<1.
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  Since $\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma}+\mathrm{e}^{-1}=1$, we obtain
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:crossing-gamma-bounds}
    g_-<\gamma<g_+.
  \end{equation}

  For $0\le t\le T$, define
  \[
    D(t)=f_\gamma(t)-\log\bigl(1+\mathrm{e}^{f_{\gamma-1}(t)}\bigr),
  \]
  where $f_z$ is the function from \cref{lem:log-power-curvature}.
  Since $\mathrm{e}^\gamma=1+\mathrm{e}^{\gamma-1}$, we have $D(0)=0$.
  For every $k\ge5$, the inequality $D(1/k)>0$ is equivalent to $g_k(\gamma+C/k)>1$.
  We will prove that $D$ is strictly concave on $[0,T]$ and $D(T)>0$.

  Set $p(t)=\mathrm{e}^{f_{\gamma-1}(t)}/(1+\mathrm{e}^{f_{\gamma-1}(t)})$.
  Differentiating $D$ twice, we obtain
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:crossing-second-derivative}
    D''(t)=f_\gamma''(t)-p(t)f_{\gamma-1}''(t)
    -p(t)(1-p(t))\bigl(f_{\gamma-1}'(t)\bigr)^2.
  \end{equation}
  We first show that $f_{\gamma-1}''(t)<0$ and $p(t)\le\rho$ on $[0,T]$.
  Since $9/20<\gamma<23/50$, we have $C>z^2/4$ for $z=\gamma,\gamma-1$.
  For $(t,s)\in[0,T]\times[0,1]$, we have $\gamma/2+Cts>0$ and $(\gamma-1)/2+Cts<0$.
  As $ts$ increases from $0$ to $T$, the square $(\gamma/2+Cts)^2$ increases and the square $((\gamma-1)/2+Cts)^2$ decreases.
  Using $9/20<\gamma<23/50$ and the values of $z/2+Cts$ for $z=\gamma,\gamma-1$ at $ts=0$ and $ts=T=1/5$, we obtain
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      \beta_\gamma^2
       & <\frac{\gamma^2}{4}
      \le (\gamma/2+Cts)^2
      \le\left(\frac\gamma2+\frac{41}{2500}\right)^2
      <3\beta_\gamma^2,                                       \\
      ((\gamma-1)/2+Cts)^2
       & \ge\left(\frac{\gamma-1}{2}+\frac{41}{2500}\right)^2
      >6\beta_{\gamma-1}^2.
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  Hence, \cref{lem:log-power-curvature}\textup{(ii),(iii)} imply $0<f_\gamma'''(t)\le3C^2$ and $f_{\gamma-1}'''(t)<0$ for $0\le t\le T$, respectively.
  By \cref{lem:log-power-curvature}\textup{(i)}, we also have $f_{\gamma-1}'(0)<0$ and $f_{\gamma-1}''(0)<0$.
  It follows that $f_{\gamma-1}'(t)<0$ and $f_{\gamma-1}''(t)<0$ throughout $[0,T]$.
  Since $f_{\gamma-1}$ decreases, we have $0<p(t)\le p(0)=\mathrm{e}^{-1}<\rho$.
  Using $f_{\gamma-1}''(t)<0$ and $0<p(t)\le\rho<1$ in \eqref{eq:crossing-second-derivative}, we obtain
  \[
    D''(t)\le f_\gamma''(t)-\rho f_{\gamma-1}''(t).
  \]
  It therefore suffices to prove $f_\gamma''(t)-\rho f_{\gamma-1}''(t)<0$ for $0\le t\le T$.

  By \cref{lem:log-power-curvature}\textup{(i)}, for $g_--1\le z\le g_+-1$ we have $-f_z'''(0)>0$ and $\frac{\partial}{\partial z}(-f_z'''(0))=6z(z^2-2C)<0$.
  The denominator $(1+zT+CT^2)^2$ is positive and increasing in $z$ on $[g_--1,g_+-1]$.
  Thus, \cref{lem:log-power-curvature}\textup{(iii)} implies, for every $t\in[0,T]$,
  \[
    0<-f_{\gamma-1}'''(t)
    \le\frac{-f_{\gamma-1}'''(0)}{(1+(\gamma-1)T+CT^2)^2}
    \le\frac{-f_{g_--1}'''(0)}{(1+(g_--1)T+CT^2)^2}
    <\frac1{150}.
  \]
  Also, $\frac{\partial}{\partial z}f_z''(0)=2(z^2-C)>0$ on both $[g_-,g_+]$ and $[g_--1,g_+-1]$.
  For every $t\in[0,T]$, integrating $f_\gamma'''(u)\le3C^2$ and $-f_{\gamma-1}'''(u)<1/150$ over $0\le u\le t$, we obtain
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:crossing-relative-curvature}
    \begin{aligned}
      f_\gamma''(t)-\rho f_{\gamma-1}''(t)
       & \le f_\gamma''(0)-\rho f_{\gamma-1}''(0)
      +t\left(3C^2+\frac\rho{150}\right)          \\
       & \le f_{g_+}''(0)-\rho f_{g_--1}''(0)
      +T\left(3C^2+\frac\rho{150}\right)
      <-\frac1{12500}.
    \end{aligned}
  \end{equation}
  By \eqref{eq:crossing-relative-curvature}, we have $D''(t)<0$ for $0\le t\le T$.

  Finally, the strict monotonicity of $g_5$ implies
  \[
    g_5(\gamma+C/5)
    >g_5(g_-+C/5)
    =\left(\frac{547507}{500000}\right)^5
    -\left(\frac{447507}{500000}\right)^5>1.
  \]
  Hence, $D(T)>0$.
  For $0<t\le T$, concavity yields
  \[
    D(t)\ge(1-t/T)D(0)+(t/T)D(T)>0.
  \]
  Thus, $g_k(\gamma+C/k)>1=g_k(c_k)$ for every $k\ge5$.
  The strict monotonicity of $g_k$ and \eqref{eq:crossing-gamma-bounds} imply $c_k<\gamma+C/k<g_++C/k$, as required.
